tamil:
குடியென்னும் குன்றா விளக்கம் மடியென்னும்
மாசூர மாய்ந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiyennum kundraa vilakkam madiyennum
Maasoora maaindhu kedum.
current_meaning: A family is like a lamp whose light should never fail, but when the grime of laziness settles on it, its light fades and goes out.
elementary_explanation: Think of a lamp that has shone in your home for years. If nobody cleans the soot off the glass, the light gets dimmer and dimmer until the room is dark. Laziness is that soot: a family stays bright only if its people keep working and caring.
university_explanation: The opening couplet sets up the chapter’s governing image: குடி (family, lineage) is a குன்றா விளக்கம், a lamp or radiance that of itself would never diminish, and மடி (sloth) is the மாசு, the grime or darkness that ‘spreads over’ (ஊர) it until it dims (மாய்ந்து) and perishes (கெடும்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read மாசு as a film of dirt that accumulates by degrees, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and the Rev. Drew/Pope tradition render it as darkness; either way the point is that decline is gradual and self-inflicted rather than sudden and external. The chapter heading மடியின்மை (‘absence of sloth’) follows ஊக்கமுடைமை (ch. 60, energy) and precedes ஆள்வினையுடைமை (ch. 62, manly effort), so Valluvar moves from the positive virtue to the vice that undoes it before turning to sustained effort. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org; the latter prints the older sandhi-joined form (விளக்க மடியென்னு / மாசூர) with no change of wording.

tamil:
மடியை மடியா ஒழுகல் குடியைக்
குடியாக வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Madiyai madiyaa ozhugal kudiyaik
Kudiyaaga vendu bavar.
current_meaning: Those who want their family to be a family in the full, honoured sense must see laziness for the ruin it is and put it to death in how they live.
elementary_explanation: If you want your team to be a real team, you can’t treat ‘I’ll do it later’ as harmless. You have to see laziness as the thing that breaks teams, and push it out every day. Families work the same way.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a double pun. மடியை மடியா can mean ‘treating sloth as sloth’, recognising it for the vice it is (Varadarasanar: சோம்பலைச் சோம்பலாகக் கொண்டு), or, because மடி also means ‘to die, perish’, ‘treating sloth as something to be killed’ or ‘as death itself’. Kalaignar’s gloss (சோம்பலை ஒழித்து) takes the second sense. The echo குடியைக் குடியாக, ‘to make the family a family’, implies that a lineage only truly exists as a குடி while it keeps its standing; Parimelazhagar takes குடி here as the illustrious family, not the bare kin-group. ஒழுகல், ‘conduct, practice’, makes this a matter of daily habit, not of a single resolution. Both source texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined மடியா வொழுகல்.

tamil:
மடிமடிக் கொண்டொழுகும் பேதை பிறந்த
குடிமடியும் தன்னினும் முந்து.
transliteration:
Madimadik kondozhugum pedhai pirandha
Kudimadiyum thanninum mundhu.
current_meaning: When a fool clings to destructive laziness, the family he was born into dies even before he does.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a boy who never helps and never learns, and lets his family’s shop fall apart. The sad part is that the shop can close long before he grows old. His laziness hurts his family first.
university_explanation: Valluvar makes மடி ring three times: மடி (sloth) … மடி … மடியும் (perishes). The phrase மடிமடிக் கொண்டு is read in two ways. Varadarasanar and Parimelazhagar take the second மடி as an adjective, ‘sloth that destroys’ (அழிக்கும் இயல்புடைய சோம்பல்). Others hear மடி in its everyday sense of ‘lap’, ‘holding sloth in his lap’, cherishing it; Pappaiah’s ‘the sloth that ought to be cast off’ is close to this. பேதை, ‘fool’, is a strong word in the Kural (see ch. 84, பேதைமை): the fault is presented as a failure of understanding, not just of energy. The paradox that the குடி dies ‘before himself’ (தன்னினும் முந்து) means that the family’s standing, its reputation and wealth, can die while its lazy member is still alive to see it. Both source texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms குடிமடியுந் தன்னினு முந்து.

tamil:
குடிமடிந்து குற்றம் பெருகும் மடிமடிந்து
மாண்ட உஞற்றி லவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kudimadindhu kutram perugum madimadindhu
Maanda unjatri lavarkku.
current_meaning: For those who sink into laziness and make no worthy effort, the family’s standing collapses and their faults keep multiplying.
elementary_explanation: When you stop doing your homework, it’s not just one problem. Soon you’re behind, you start making excuses, and you get into more trouble. Laziness is like a door that lets many other problems in, and the whole family feels it.
university_explanation: The couplet names two consequences: குடி மடிந்து, ‘the family perishing’, and குற்றம் பெருகும், ‘faults multiplying’. It gives one cause: மடி மடிந்து, ‘having fallen into sloth’. Here மடிந்து is used in the sense of ‘sinking’ or ‘being caught’, which Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss as சோம்பலில் அகப்பட்டு / வீழ்வதால். The rare word உஞற்று (effort, exertion) together with மாண்ட (excellent, worthy) specifies what is missing: not activity of any kind but dignified, purposeful effort (Pope’s ‘noble objects’). Parimelazhagar notes that idleness is productive, of vice, which fits a line of Indian moral thought in which inactivity invites other faults. The same second-line phrase recurs in 607 (மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர்), which ties the two couplets together. Both sources agree; the older text has the sandhi forms பெருகு மடிமடிந்து and மாண்ட வுஞற்றி.

tamil:
நெடுநீர் மறவி மடிதுயில் நான்கும்
கெடுநீரார் காமக் கலன்.
transliteration:
Neduneer maravi madidhuyil naangum
Keduneeraar kaamak kalan.
current_meaning: Procrastination, forgetfulness, laziness and oversleeping are the four things people bound for ruin love to board, like a pleasure boat carrying them to disaster.
elementary_explanation: Imagine four friends who always say: ‘Do it later’, ‘Oops, I forgot’, ‘I’m too tired’, and ‘Just five more minutes of sleep.’ They feel comfy, like a boat ride, but the boat is floating toward a waterfall. Good habits are how you steer the boat back.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s best-known couplet and its most careful analysis. It lists four linked dispositions: நெடுநீர், literally ‘long-drawn nature’, i.e. procrastination (Varadarasanar: காலம் நீட்டித்தல்); மறவி, forgetfulness or heedlessness (compare ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை); மடி, sloth; and துயில், excessive sleep. It calls them the காமக் கலன் of the கெடுநீரார், ‘those whose nature is to perish’. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators take கலன் as a vessel or ship (மரக்கலம்; Pappaiah: சிறு படகு), giving Pope’s ‘pleasure-boat … to ruin’s shore’. Because கலன் can also mean ‘ornament’, some readers take the line as ‘the ornaments the doomed love to wear’, but the vessel reading is standard. The rhyme நெடுநீர் / கெடுநீரார் binds cause to result. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s gloss of நெடுநீர் as ‘long weeping’ is idiosyncratic and not followed by the classical commentators. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (மடிதுயி னான்குங்).

tamil:
படியுடையார் பற்றமைந்தக் கண்ணும் மடியுடையார்
மாண்பயன் எய்தல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Padiyudaiyaar patramaindhak kannum madiyudaiyaar
Maanpayan eydhal aridhu.
current_meaning: Even if the lazy come into the wealth of kings who ruled the whole earth, they will rarely get any real good out of it.
elementary_explanation: Suppose someone gives you the world’s biggest box of Lego but you never open it. You own it, but you never build anything. Having great things doesn’t help if you’re too lazy to use them.
university_explanation: படி here means ‘the earth’, so படியுடையார் are ‘those who possess the earth’, world-ruling kings. பற்று அமைதல் is ‘their possessions or support coming to one’. The classical reading (Parimelazhagar, Varadarasanar, Pappaiah) is: even if the whole wealth of such sovereigns comes to the lazy, they will rarely obtain மாண்பயன், its excellent fruit. Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read படியுடையார் as ‘worthy or powerful persons’ and பற்று as their affection or patronage: even with the favour of the great, the idle will not rise. The two readings share the same moral: fortune and connection are worthless without exertion. The couplet anticipates 610, where the tireless king gains all that Vishnu’s stride covered, and together they frame the second half of the chapter. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (கண்ணு மடியுடையார் / மாண்பய னெய்த லரிது).

tamil:
இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளுஞ்சொல் கேட்பர் மடிபுரிந்து
மாண்ட உஞற்றி லவர்.
transliteration:
Idipurindhu ellunjol ketpar madipurindhu
Maanda unjatri lavar.
current_meaning: Those who give themselves to laziness and make no worthy effort will have to hear harsh rebukes and scornful words.
elementary_explanation: When you promise to help clean up and then just lie on the couch, first your friends say, ‘Come on, help!’ If you still don’t, they start to laugh at you or stop counting on you. Laziness turns friends’ nudges into teasing.
university_explanation: இடிபுரிந்து எள்ளும் சொல் combines two kinds of speech: இடி, sharp rebuke (the verb இடித்தல் is used elsewhere in the Kural for a true friend’s correction, e.g. ch. 45, 448), and எள்ளல், scornful mockery. Pappaiah and Parimelazhagar read them as a sequence: friends first rebuke the idle man, and when that fails, contempt follows. மடிபுரிந்து, ‘having embraced sloth by choice’, stresses that the laziness is willed, and the second line repeats the மாண்ட உஞற்றிலவர் of 604, so this couplet adds a social consequence (loss of respect) to the material one described there. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இடிபுரிந்து as ‘slipping and falling’, a minority interpretation. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form இடிபுரிந் தெள்ளுஞ்சொற் கேட்பர்.

tamil:
மடிமை குடிமைக்கண் தங்கின்தன் ஒன்னார்க்கு
அடிமை புகுத்தி விடும்.
transliteration:
Madimai kudimaikkan thangindhan onnaarkku
Adimai pugutthi vidum.
current_meaning: If laziness settles in someone of noble birth, it will end by making him a slave to his own enemies.
elementary_explanation: A castle with strong walls is safe only while its guards stay awake. If the guards get lazy and fall asleep, the enemy walks right in. Being from a great family won’t protect you if laziness moves in.
university_explanation: The couplet depends on a rhyme chain: மடிமை (sloth), குடிமை (nobility of birth), அடிமை (slavery). The sound itself follows the slide from high birth through sloth into bondage. தங்கின், ‘if it takes up residence’, presents sloth as a lodger that gradually takes over the house. ஒன்னார், ‘those who are not one with you’, i.e. enemies, and புகுத்திவிடும், ‘will thrust one into’, give the outcome. Pope’s rendering (‘Bondsmen to them that hate them shall they be’) and the Drew-Lazarus gloss both take the subject as a king of high birth, which fits the placement of the chapter in the அரசியல் (polity) section. Parimelazhagar notes that the sloth of a ruler becomes his enemies’ opportunity. The older text shows heavy sandhi (குடிமைக்கட் டங்கிற்றன் னொன்னார்க் / கடிமை) without any change in wording.

tamil:
குடியாண்மை யுள்வந்த குற்றம் ஒருவன்
மடியாண்மை மாற்றக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiyaanmai yulvandha kutram oruvan
Madiyaanmai maatrak kedum.
current_meaning: When a person throws off the rule that laziness has over him, the faults that had crept into his family and his own manhood disappear.
elementary_explanation: If your room has become a mess because you kept putting things off, you don’t need magic. Start tidying today and the mess goes away. Kick out laziness and good things come back.
university_explanation: After the warnings of 601-608, the ninth couplet offers a remedy, built on the parallel compounds குடியாண்மை and மடியாண்மை. The first is read either as குடி + ஆண்மை, ‘family and manly worth’ (Varadarasanar: குடியிலும் ஆண்மையிலும்; Kalaignar: குடிப்பெருமைக்கும் ஆண்மைக்கும்), or as ‘the governing of one’s family’. The second, மடி + ஆண்மை, is ironic: sloth exercising ‘lordship’ (ஆண்மை) over a man, so that he is its subject (Pappaiah: சோம்பலுக்கு அடிமையாவது). மாற்ற, ‘when one changes, reverses’, puts the cure in the person’s own hands. Echoing 608, where sloth makes a man a slave, here overthrowing sloth’s rule restores him. The older text reads குற்ற மொருவன் with no change of sense.

tamil:
மடியிலா மன்னவன் எய்தும் அடியளந்தான்
தாஅய தெல்லாம் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Madiyilaa mannavan eydhum adiyalandhaan
Thaaaya thellaam orungu.
current_meaning: A king free of laziness will gain, all at once, the whole of what the God who measured the worlds with his feet strode across.
elementary_explanation: There is an old story about a god who grew so tall that he crossed the whole world in a few giant steps. This kural says a leader who is never lazy can, by working hard, win everything those giant steps covered. Hard work lets small people take giant steps too.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a Puranic allusion. அடியளந்தான், ‘he who measured with his foot’, is Vishnu as Vāmana-Trivikrama, the dwarf who asked King Mahābali for three paces of land and then grew to cover earth and heaven. தாஅயது (with அளபெடை, vowel lengthening, of தாயது, ‘what he strode across’) is therefore the whole cosmos. ஒருங்கு, ‘together, at once’, suggests that the energetic king gains all of it at once rather than piece by piece. Parimelazhagar and Varadarasanar read it this way; Kalaignar rationalises the image into a king bringing all he traverses under his footprint. The couplet balances 606: there the idle inherit world-rulers’ wealth and gain nothing, here the tireless king gains the world. The older text has the sandhi-joined form அடியளந்தான் றாஅய தெல்லா மொருங்கு, which differs from the ytamizh reading only in how the words are split.

tamil:
அருமை உடைத்தென்று அசாவாமை வேண்டும்
பெருமை முயற்சி தரும்.
transliteration:
Arumai udaiththendru asaavaamai vendum
Perumai muyarchi tharum.
current_meaning: Never lose heart by telling yourself a task is too hard; it is effort itself that gives you the strength and stature to carry it through.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a big hill you have to climb to get home. If you stand at the bottom saying 'it’s too steep,' you never move. But every step you take makes your legs a little stronger, until the hill doesn’t look so big any more. Trying is what makes you able.
university_explanation: The chapter title ஆள்வினை (literally ‘man-work’, human exertion) is glossed by the Thirukkural-Thamizh edition as இடைவிடாத முயற்சி, ‘unceasing effort’, and this opening couplet names the first enemy of effort: அசாவு, the despondency that sets in when a task is judged அருமை (difficult). Parimelazhagar takes பெருமை not as fame but as the ‘greatness’ or capacity needed to accomplish the deed, so the claim is causal: capacity is produced by striving rather than being a precondition for it; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah (ytamizh.com) both read it this way, while Kalaignar renders பெருமை as ‘great strength’. Placed immediately after ஊக்கமுடைமை (ch. 60, energy) and மடியின்மை (ch. 61, absence of sloth), the chapter moves from inner zeal to its outward expression in sustained work, culminating in the famous claim of kural 620 that effort can turn back fate itself. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (அருமை யுடைத்தென் றசாவாமை).

tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினைகெடல் ஓம்பல் வினைக்குறை
தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று உலகு.
transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaikedal ombal vinaikkurai
Theerndhaarin theerndhandru ulagu.
current_meaning: Once you are in the middle of a task, guard against letting your effort slacken; the world abandons those who abandon their work half-done.
elementary_explanation: If you start building a sandcastle and walk away halfway, the waves wash it away and nobody even knows what you were making. Friends want to team up with the kid who finishes things. Keep going until it’s done.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on வினை three times: in the course of வினை (the undertaking), guard against கெடல் (the failing) of வினை (the exertion), because the world has already தீர்ந்தது (let go of) those who have let go of வினைக்குறை, the unfinished remainder of the work. Parimelazhagar reads the first வினை as the undertaking and the second as the effort (முயற்சி), which Mu. Varadarasanar follows; Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases the rhetorical jingle of the second line (தீர்ந்தாரின் தீர்ந்தன்று) as ‘the world lets go of those who let go’. Kalaignar glosses it with the proverb of the man who ‘leapt half-way across the well’, a vivid way of saying that half an effort is no effort at all. The text agrees in both editions consulted, thirukkural-thamizh.org merely printing the sandhi forms வினைகெட லோம்பல் and தீர்ந்தாரிற் றீர்ந்தன் றுலகு.

tamil:
தாளாண்மை என்னும் தகைமைக்கண் தங்கிற்றே
வேளாண்மை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Thaalaanmai ennum thagaimaikkan thangitre
Velaanmai ennum serukku.
current_meaning: The proud distinction of being able to help others rests on one foundation only: the noble quality of hard work.
elementary_explanation: You can only share cookies with your friends if somebody baked them first. People who work hard are the ones who end up with something to give, and giving feels great. So working is what makes kindness possible.
university_explanation: தாளாண்மை, literally ‘the rule of the foot’, is Valluvar’s image for vigorous exertion, and வேளாண்மை here means beneficence or generosity to others (Parimelazhagar: உபகாரம்), not ‘agriculture’, its commonest modern sense. செருக்கு, usually ‘arrogance’, is used positively for the lofty eminence or noble pride of a benefactor, and the emphatic particle ஏ in தங்கிற்றே (‘it abides only there’) makes effort the exclusive seat of that eminence. The logic, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both preserve, links this chapter to the Arathuppal chapters on ஒப்புரவறிதல் and ஈகை: generosity is a virtue, but it presupposes the means that only labour produces. Kalaignar reads the couplet as describing people of ‘unceasing effort’ in whom the pride of helping others takes root. Both editions consulted agree on the text, apart from sandhi (தகைமைக்கட் டங்கிற்றே).

tamil:
தாளாண்மை இல்லாதான் வேளாண்மை பேடிகை
வாளாண்மை போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Thaalaanmai illaadhaan velaanmai pedikai
Vaalaanmai polak kedum.
current_meaning: A person who will not work but wants to be generous will fail, like a sword brandished by someone with no stomach for battle.
elementary_explanation: Holding a toy sword doesn’t make you a knight; you need the courage to use it. In the same way, saying ‘I’ll help everyone!’ doesn’t help anyone unless you are willing to do the work that makes helping possible.
university_explanation: The couplet sharpens kural 613 by negation: வேளாண்மை (beneficence) without தாளாண்மை (effort) is like the வாளாண்மை (sword-mastery) of a பேடி. Parimelazhagar and the older commentators take பேடி as a person of indeterminate sex, conventionally assumed in the ancient world to lack a warrior’s daring; Solomon Pappaiah softens this to ‘one who trembles at the sight of an army’, and the image is best read today as ‘a sword in the hand of one who dare not use it’, since the underlying gender assumption reflects its period rather than Valluvar’s point. The logic is that good intentions without the means produced by labour are as useless as a weapon one cannot wield; Mu. Varadarasanar says such generosity ‘will not come to fulfilment’. Both editions consulted agree on the wording; the sandhi form தாளாண்மை யில்லாதான் is purely orthographic.

tamil:
இன்பம் விழையான் வினைவிழைவான் தன்கேளிர்
துன்பம் துடைத்தூன்றும் தூண்.
transliteration:
Inbam vizhaiyaan vinaivizhaivaan thankelir
Thunbam thudaiththoondrum thoon.
current_meaning: Someone who wants work rather than personal pleasure becomes a pillar for their family, wiping away their troubles and holding them up.
elementary_explanation: A house stands because of its pillars. They never get to go out and play; they just hold up the roof so everyone inside is safe. A person who chooses to work hard instead of just having fun becomes a pillar like that for their family.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts two desires: இன்பம் விழையான் (one who does not crave his own pleasure) and வினை விழைவான் (one who craves the work). Such a man is a தூண் (pillar) that both துடைத்து (wipes away) and ஊன்றும் (props up) the sorrows of his கேளிர், his kin; Solomon Pappaiah widens கேளிர் to ‘relatives and friends’ and Kalaignar extends it to ‘the people of the country’, a modern civic reading. Parimelazhagar notes that the pillar image implies a household or lineage that would collapse without such a person. The couplet echoes the Arathuppal ideal of the householder (இல்வாழ்க்கை) as the support of all dependants, now reframed as a fruit of personal effort. Both editions agree on the wording, with sandhi-joined forms (வினைவிழைவான் றன்கேளிர்; துன்பந் துடைத்தூன்றுந் தூண்).

tamil:
முயற்சி திருவினை ஆக்கும் முயற்றின்மை
இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்.
transliteration:
Muyarchi thiruvinai aakkum muyatrinmai
Inmai puguththi vidum.
current_meaning: Effort builds up prosperity; lack of effort ushers poverty in.
elementary_explanation: If you water a plant every day, it grows and gives you flowers. If you forget, it dries up. Effort is the water that makes good things grow, and not trying lets things wilt.
university_explanation: This is perhaps the most quoted couplet of the chapter, built on the paired opposites முயற்சி / முயற்றின்மை and ஆக்கும் / புகுத்திவிடும். Parimelazhagar reads திருவினை as திரு (wealth, prosperity) plus the empty increment இன் and the accusative ஐ, so ‘effort creates wealth’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this, whereas Sivayogi Sivakumar splits it as திரு + வினை, ‘auspicious deeds’, and Kalaignar as ‘excellent achievements’. இன்மை, ‘non-being’, is the standard Kural word for poverty (compare ch. 105, நல்குரவு), and புகுத்திவிடும் pictures idleness as actively ushering poverty into the house. The text is identical in both editions, thirukkural-thamizh.org printing the sandhi forms திருவினை யாக்கும் and யின்மை.

tamil:
மடியுளாள் மாமுகடி என்ப மடியிலான்
தாளுளாள் தாமரையி னாள்.
transliteration:
Madiyulaal maamugadi enba madiyilaan
Thaalulaal thaamaraiyinaal.
current_meaning: The wise say the dark goddess of misfortune lives in laziness, while the lotus-goddess of fortune lives in the effort of the one who is not lazy.
elementary_explanation: Pretend Good Luck and Bad Luck are two visitors looking for a home. Bad Luck loves a messy room where someone is napping all day. Good Luck knocks on the door of the kid who’s busy building and practising. Where you work, good luck moves in.
university_explanation: Valluvar borrows two goddesses of popular belief: மாமுகடி, the ‘great dark Mugadi’ (மூதேவி, Sanskrit Jyeṣṭhā or Alakṣmī), goddess of misfortune, and தாமரையினாள், ‘she of the lotus’, Tirumagal or Lakshmi; the verb என்ப (‘they say’) signals that he is citing received wisdom. Parimelazhagar notes that sloth is the ‘dwelling’ of the one and effort (தாள்) the dwelling of the other, so fortune is located not in fate but in conduct; Kalaignar demythologises the pair entirely, treating the goddess names as figures for the industrious and the idle. There is a textual point: ytamizh.com prints தாளுளான் (masculine), but the parallelism with மடியுளாள் and the sandhi form றாளுளா டாமரையி னாள் in thirukkural-thamizh.org (தாளுளாள் + தாமரை) confirm the feminine தாளுளாள், ‘she dwells in the effort’, which is the reading adopted here.

tamil:
பொறியின்மை யார்க்கும் பழியன்று அறிவறிந்து
ஆள்வினை இன்மை பழி.
transliteration:
Poriyinmai yaarkkum pazhiyandru arivarindhu
Aalvinai inmai pazhi.
current_meaning: Bad luck is no disgrace to anyone; the real disgrace is knowing what should be done and still not making the effort.
elementary_explanation: Nobody laughs at you if it rains on sports day. That’s just bad luck. But if you knew you had a test and didn’t study at all, that’s on you. What matters is whether you tried.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on பழி (blame, disgrace) and on the contested word பொறி. Parimelazhagar takes பொறி as ஊழ், favourable destiny, so ‘to lack good fortune is no disgrace’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow him, while Solomon Pappaiah (and, differently, Sivayogi Sivakumar) read பொறி in its other sense of bodily organ or faculty, making the point that physical disability is no disgrace but failure to exert oneself is. Both readings yield the same moral: blame attaches only to what lies in our power, namely அறிவறிந்து ஆள்வினை, effort guided by knowing what ought to be known. The chapter title word ஆள்வினை appears here explicitly, and the couplet prepares for 619-620’s direct confrontation with fate. The text is the same in both editions (sandhi: பழியன் றறிவறிந் / தாள்வினை யின்மை).

tamil:
தெய்வத்தான் ஆகா தெனினும் முயற்சிதன்
மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்.
transliteration:
Theyvaththaan aagaadhu eninum muyarchithan
Meyvaruththak kooli tharum.
current_meaning: Even if fate keeps the goal from being reached, effort will still pay the wages of the body’s toil.
elementary_explanation: Say you practise hard for a race and still don’t win because it rained and you slipped. You didn’t get the trophy, but your legs are stronger and you’re faster than before. Hard work always pays something, even when luck says no.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar glosses தெய்வம் as ஊழ் (fate, the fruit of past deeds), so the protasis concedes that destiny may make the full aim unattainable (ஆகாது); even then முயற்சி pays தன் மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி, the wage owed for its own bodily strain. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah keep the fate reading, but Kalaignar takes தெய்வம் literally as God, turning the couplet into a rationalist contrast between calling on God and working, a reading the Tamil can bear but the commentarial tradition does not support. The couplet is a careful concession to chapter 38 (ஊழ்), where kural 380 asks what is stronger than fate: Valluvar grants fate’s power over outcomes while denying it power to cancel the return on labour. Both editions agree, thirukkural-thamizh.org printing தெய்வத்தா னாகா தெனினு முயற்சிதன்.

tamil:
ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர் உலைவின்றித்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்.
transliteration:
Oozhaiyum uppakkam kaanbar ulaivindrith
Thaazhaadhu unjatru bavar.
current_meaning: Those who strive without faltering and without slackening will see even fate turn its back and retreat.
elementary_explanation: Think of a tiny stream running into a big rock. The rock seems stronger, but the water keeps flowing, day after day, until it carves a path around or even through. People who keep going without giving up can get past even the biggest ‘it’s just meant to be’.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with its boldest claim, the one most often quoted: tireless strivers will காண்பர் (see) the உப்பக்கம் (back, rear side) of ஊழ் (fate) itself, a battlefield image of an enemy turning its back in flight (Solomon Pappaiah: விதியையும் புறமுதுகு காட்டக் காண்பர்). The conditions are exacting: உலைவின்றி (without wavering), தாழாது (without delay or slackening) and உஞற்றுபவர் (those who exert themselves, an old verb for effort). Because chapter 38 insists on ஊழின் பெருவலி (fate’s great strength, kural 380), commentators have laboured to reconcile the two; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar soften the claim so that strivers defeat the fate that obstructs a particular undertaking ‘in time’, while Kalaignar reads it as an outright rejection of fatalism. The couplet stands in the same Indian debate as the Mahabharata’s daiva-versus-puruṣakāra discussions and the Yoga Vasishtha’s praise of paurusha; the text agrees in both editions (sandhi: ஊழையு முப்பக்கங் காண்ப ருலைவின்றித் / தாழா துஞற்று பவர்).

tamil:
இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக அதனை
அடுத்தூர்வது அஃதொப்ப தில்.
transliteration:
Itukkan varungaal nakuka adhanai
Atuththoorvadhu aqdhoppa thil.
current_meaning: When trouble comes, meet it with a smile; nothing presses upon trouble and overpowers it as well as that cheerful calm does.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your sandcastle gets knocked over by a wave. You can cry, or you can laugh and start building again. The Kural says the laugh is the strongest tool you have: a cheerful heart beats trouble better than anything else.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with its most famous imperative, nakuka (laugh, smile), which the commentators do not read as mockery but as the outward sign of a mind that refuses to be shaken; Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as rejoicing inwardly, Mu. Varadarasanar as not being agitated. The second line turns on aṭuttūrvatu, literally ‘that which presses close and rides over’, a verbal noun describing what can close in on sorrow and subdue it, and aḥtoppatu il says nothing equals ‘that’ (the laughter or the unperturbed state it expresses). Parimelazhagar, whose commentary frames Idukkan Azhiyaamai as the natural sequel to the preceding chapter on sustained effort (Aalvinaiyudaimai), understands the troubles here as those that arise in the course of undertaking great works, so the king or doer must not lose heart midway. The couplet text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh writes the chapter title as one word, இடுக்கணழியாமை, and thirukkural.net renders it ‘Not despairing in afflictive times’, while Pope’s title is ‘Hopefulness in Trouble’.

tamil:
வெள்ளத் தனைய இடும்பை அறிவுடையான்
உள்ளத்தின் உள்ளக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Vellath thanaiya itumpai arivutaiyaan
Ullaththin ullak ketum.
current_meaning: Even a sorrow as vast as a flood is destroyed the moment a wise person turns a steady mind upon it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a huge wave rushing at a beach. It looks scary, but when it hits a strong rock it just breaks into foam. A wise, calm mind is like that rock: even a flood of problems falls apart when it meets clear, brave thinking.
university_explanation: The flood simile (veḷḷattaṉaiya, ‘flood-like’) stresses both the size and the sudden, overwhelming onrush of trouble (iṭumpai). The second line plays on uḷḷam (mind) and uḷḷa (to think, to resolve): the trouble perishes (keṭum) merely by the wise man’s mind thinking upon it, which Mu. Varadarasanar explains as reflecting on the nature of the trouble, and Solomon Pappaiah as the mind refusing to slacken. Parimelazhagar and later commentators read uḷḷam here as close to ūkkam, the mental elation or resolve praised in chapter 60, so that one act of firm resolve dissolves a whole flood of difficulty. The text agrees in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, and Pope’s rendering (‘When wise men’s mind regards it, it is gone’) follows the same construal.

tamil:
இடும்பைக்கு இடும்பை படுப்பர் இடும்பைக்கு
இடும்பை படாஅ தவர்.
transliteration:
Itumpaikku itumpai patuppar itumpaikku
Itumpai pataaa thavar.
current_meaning: Those who do not let sorrow grieve them turn the tables and bring grief upon sorrow itself.
elementary_explanation: A bully loves it when you get upset. If you stay calm and cheerful, the bully gets frustrated and gives up. Trouble is like that bully: if you refuse to be sad about it, the trouble is the one that ends up losing.
university_explanation: This couplet is a celebrated piece of Valluvar’s wordplay: iṭumpai (sorrow, affliction) occurs four times, arranged chiastically so that ‘those who do not suffer sorrow for sorrow’ are said to ‘cause sorrow to sorrow’. The form paṭā’a in the second line is an alapedai (metrical lengthening, அளபெடை), marked in thirukkural.net’s romanisation as paṭā'a and preserved in both sources consulted. The personification of trouble as an opponent who can itself be defeated recurs in 624 and 625, making the triad the rhetorical centre of the chapter; Parimelazhagar’s line of interpretation, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar, is that the undaunted person so frustrates misfortune that it withdraws defeated. Pope’s version, ‘From them griefs, put to grief, depart’, keeps the paronomasia.

tamil:
மடுத்தவா யெல்லாம் பகடன்னான் உற்ற
இடுக்கண் இடர்ப்பாடு உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Matuththavaa yellaam pakatannaan utra
Itukkan itarppaatu utaiththu.
current_meaning: The trouble that meets a person who, like an ox, keeps hauling the cart through every rut and mire will itself be the one that suffers.
elementary_explanation: Picture a strong ox pulling a heavy cart down a muddy road. Every time a wheel gets stuck, the ox just leans in and pulls harder until it’s free. If you keep going like that ox, your problems get tired before you do.
university_explanation: Maṭuttavāy ellām means ‘in all the places where (the cart) sinks or is blocked’, from maṭu, a pit or deep hollow, and the image is completed by pakaṭu, a draught ox or bull that pulls the cart out without flinching; Pope’s explanation renders pakaṭu as ‘buffalo … through deep mire’, reflecting a traditional alternative gloss for the animal. The second line again personifies trouble: the iṭukkaṇ that such a person meets ‘itself suffers hardship’ (iṭarppāṭu uṭaittu). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both stress persistence without losing heart, while Kalaignar expands the image into success through unbroken effort, linking this couplet to the doctrine of ūkkam and āḷviṉai in chapters 60 and 62. The text is the same in both sources; ytamizh prints the sandhi form மடுத்தவா யெல்லாம் exactly as thirukkural.net does.

tamil:
அடுக்கி வரினும் அழிவிலான் உற்ற
இடுக்கண் இடுக்கட் படும்.
transliteration:
Atukki varinum azhivilaan utra
Itukkan itukkat patum.
current_meaning: Even if troubles come piled one upon another, the troubles of a person who does not break inside are the ones that end up in trouble.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes bad things come in a row, like missing the bus, then spilling your lunch, then losing your pencil. If you keep your spirit strong and don’t give up, all those troubles run out of steam, one after another.
university_explanation: Aṭukki varinum, ‘even if they come stacked’, answers the natural objection to 623 and 624: what if troubles do not come singly but in a relentless series? The subject aḻivilāṉ is literally ‘one without destruction’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss as one whose mind does not collapse (kalaṅkāmal, maṉam taḷarātavaṉ). The closing iṭukkaṇ iṭukkaṭ paṭum repeats the reversal of 623 with iṭukkaṇ instead of iṭumpai, the sandhi iṭukkaṭ reflecting the following p-. Both sources agree on the text, and the commentarial tradition treats 623-625 as a graded sequence: undaunted by one trouble, dragging through many ruts, and unbroken even by a pile of calamities.

tamil:
அற்றேமென்று அல்லற் படுபவோ பெற்றேமென்று
ஓம்புதல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Atremendru allar patupavo petremendru
Ompudhal thetraa thavar.
current_meaning: Would those who never clung anxiously to their wealth, saying ‘we have it’, ever wail ‘we have lost everything’ when it goes?
elementary_explanation: If you share your toys freely and don’t get too attached to them, you won’t cry much when one breaks. The Kural says people who didn’t cling to their riches don’t fall apart when the riches are gone.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two first-person plural verbs against each other: aṟṟēm, ‘we are bereft’, and peṟṟēm, ‘we have obtained’, the first the cry of the ruined man, the second the self-congratulation of the prosperous. Ōmputal tēṟṟātavar, ‘those who do not know (or care) to hoard and guard’, is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as those who did not greedily cling to wealth when they had it, while Solomon Pappaiah takes it as those who freely gave it away to others, and Kalaignar as those who were not elated by it; the three glosses share the idea that detachment in prosperity prevents despair in loss. The rhetorical question (paṭupavō, ‘would they suffer?’) expects the answer no, and the text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The couplet shifts the chapter from enduring trouble to preventing it inwardly, preparing for the equanimity teaching of 627-629.

tamil:
இலக்கம் உடம்பிடும்பைக் கென்று கலக்கத்தைக்
கையாறாக் கொள்ளாதாம் மேல்.
transliteration:
Ilakkam utampitumpaik kendru kalakkaththaik
Kaiyaaraak kollaadhaam mel.
current_meaning: Knowing that the body is simply a target for pain, the noble do not treat the agitation it brings as a real calamity.
elementary_explanation: A football goal is made to have balls kicked at it; nobody is shocked when a ball hits it. The Kural says our bodies are a bit like that: bumps, colds and aches are bound to come, so wise people don’t panic when they do.
university_explanation: Ilakkam (from ilakku, ‘target’, cognate with Sanskrit lakṣya) makes the body the mark at which afflictions are aimed, an idea the commentators connect with the inevitability of bodily pain for every embodied being. Kalakkam is inner agitation, and kaiyāṟu is a rarer word that the traditional commentary takes as distress or helpless grief, so that the great ‘do not take agitation as (a cause of) distress’; Mu. Varadarasanar instead renders the construction as not adopting agitation as their way of conduct, showing a genuine interpretive divergence. Mēl, ‘the superior ones’, is the subject, with the verb in the honorific-epicene form koḷḷātām. The text is identical in both sources consulted, and Pope’s ‘Man’s frame is sorrow’s target, the noble mind reflects’ keeps the reasoning explicit.

tamil:
இன்பம் விழையான் இடும்பை இயல்பென்பான்
துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்.
transliteration:
Inpam vizhaiyaan itumpai iyalpenpaan
Thunpam urudhal ilan.
current_meaning: One who does not chase after pleasure and who accepts hardship as a natural part of life never really falls into misery.
elementary_explanation: If you expect every day to be a party, a rainy day feels awful. But if you know that some days are rainy and that’s normal, you just grab an umbrella. The Kural says people who don’t demand fun all the time don’t get crushed when hard times come.
university_explanation: The couplet pairs two participial nouns, iṉpam viḻaiyāṉ, ‘one who does not crave pleasure’, and iṭumpai iyalpeṉpāṉ, ‘one who says hardship is natural (iyalpu)’, and concludes that such a person ‘has no falling into sorrow’ (tuṉpam uṟutal ilaṉ). Solomon Pappaiah restricts the pleasure in question to bodily pleasure, in line with 627’s focus on the body, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as not roaming in search of enjoyment. The shift from iṭumpai (hardship, the event) to tuṉpam (suffering, the experience) is significant: hardship still comes, but it no longer becomes suffering. The text is the same in both sources, and Pope renders it ‘He seeks not joy, to sorrow man is born, he knows’.

tamil:
இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான் துன்பத்துள்
துன்பம் உறுதல் இலன்.
transliteration:
Inpaththul inpam vizhaiyaadhaan thunpaththul
Thunpam urudhal ilan.
current_meaning: One who does not greedily revel in pleasure when times are good will not be sunk in sorrow when times are bad.
elementary_explanation: If you jump up and down screaming when you win a game, you might cry just as hard when you lose. But if you enjoy the win calmly, you can handle the loss calmly too. The Kural says staying balanced in good times keeps you steady in bad times.
university_explanation: The couplet is built as a strict parallel, iṉpattuḷ iṉpam / tuṉpattuḷ tuṉpam, ‘in pleasure, pleasure’ and ‘in sorrow, sorrow’, so that the inner response mirrors the outer situation in each case. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first half as not cherishing and clinging to pleasure when it comes, and Kalaignar summarises it with a Tamil jingle, not dancing in joy and not wilting in sorrow, as an example of regarding both alike. It differs from 628 in that it concerns one’s attitude within pleasure already present rather than the pursuit of pleasure. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, and Pope’s ‘Mid joys he yields not heart to joys’ control’ captures the sense of inner restraint.

tamil:
இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின் ஆகுந்தன்
ஒன்னார் விழையுஞ் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Innaamai inpam enakkolin aakundhan
Onnaar vizhaiyunj chirappu.
current_meaning: If a person can take hardship as though it were pleasure, he will win a distinction that even his enemies will admire and desire.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a runner who smiles even while climbing the steepest hill in a race. Even the runners from the other team end up cheering for her. The Kural says if you can treat hard work and hard times as something good, even people who don’t like you will respect you.
university_explanation: Iṉṉāmai, ‘the unpleasant, pain’, is the negative of iṉṉā (sweet), so the couplet literally asks one to count the un-sweet as sweet (iṉpam eṉakkoḷiṉ). The reward is ciṟappu, eminence or distinction, qualified as oṉṉār viḻaiyum, ‘which even foes (oṉṉār, those not at one with us) desire or esteem’; ākuntaṉ is ākum taṉ with the final m assimilated, and viḻaiyuñ likewise before ciṟappu. Solomon Pappaiah specifies the hardship as that met while carrying out an undertaking, keeping the chapter’s Parimelazhagar-style link to the king’s or doer’s enterprise, while Mu. Varadarasanar reads it generally. The two sources agree on the text, and the couplet closes the chapter by turning the whole theme outward: inner mastery of trouble becomes public honour.

tamil:
கருவியும் காலமும் செய்கையும் செய்யும்
அருவினையும் மாண்டது அமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Karuviyum kaalamum seykaiyum seyyum
Aruvinaiyum maandadhu amaichchu.
current_meaning: A true minister is one who excels at thinking through the means needed, the right time, the method of doing it, and the difficult task itself.
elementary_explanation: Think of a team captain planning a school play. A good captain asks: what props do we need, when should we rehearse, how should we do each scene, and what is the hardest part? This kural says a good adviser always thinks about all four of those things.
university_explanation: The couplet opens the Amaichiyal (the section on ministers, chapters 64-73) by defining the minister (amaichu, an abstract noun used for the office-holder) through four objects of deliberation: karuvi (instruments or means, which commentators gloss as troops and wealth), kaalam (the fitting time), seykai (the mode or method of execution) and seyyum aruvinai (the difficult undertaking to be carried out). The verb maandadhu (‘excels, is perfected in’) makes the definition a standard of excellence, not merely a job description. Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Mu. Varadarasanar read the list as the components of good counsel, which lines up closely with Kautilya’s five limbs of mantra (Arthashastra 1.15). The text is stable across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org edition, where it appears as ‘karuviyum kaalamum seykaiyum seyyu / maruvinaiyu maanda thamaichchu’. The difference is only in how the words are split; the reading is the same.

tamil:
வன்கண் குடிகாத்தல் கற்றறிதல் ஆள்வினையோடு
ஐந்துடன் மாண்டது அமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Vankan kudikaaththal katrarithal aalvinaiyodu
Aindhudan maandadhu amaichchu.
current_meaning: A minister excels in firm courage, protecting the people, learning and understanding, and persevering effort, together with the five qualities already named.
elementary_explanation: A good class monitor is brave enough to speak up, looks after classmates, keeps learning, and does not give up when a job gets hard. This kural says a good adviser needs all of these together, not just one.
university_explanation: The couplet names further qualities: vankan (firmness or fearlessness, literally ‘hard eye’), kudikaaththal (protecting the subjects), katrarithal (knowing through study), and aalvinai (sustained effort, the subject of chapter 62). The phrase aindhudan (‘with the five’) is read in more than one way. In the Parimelazhagar tradition it refers back to the qualities already listed, so the minister has these as well as those. Mu. Varadarasanar splits kudi as noble birth (kudippirappu) and kaaththal as protection so that the verse itself lists five. Puliyur Kesikan instead takes the five as the purity of the five senses. Solomon Pappaiah divides katru and arithal into learning from books and learning by listening to the learned. The older-orthography edition prints ‘katrarithalaalvinaiyo / daindhudan’, which is the same text with a different word division.

tamil:
பிரித்தலும் பேணிக் கொளலும் பிரிந்தார்ப்
பொருத்தலும் வல்ல தமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Piriththalum paenik kolalum pirindhaarp
Poruththalum valla thamaichchu.
current_meaning: A minister is skilled at splitting the enemy’s allies away, keeping his own side loyal, and bringing back those who have broken away.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two teams in a playground game. A clever captain can persuade kids who are thinking of joining the other team to stay neutral, keep his own teammates happy, and make friends again with anyone who left in a huff. This kural says a good adviser has those three skills.
university_explanation: The couplet names three diplomatic skills. Piriththal is detaching allies from the enemy. Paenik kolal is keeping one’s own supporters, which Solomon Pappaiah explains as keeping them through gifts and kind words. Pirindhaar poruththal is reconciling those who have left. Commentators link these to the classical upayas (means of statecraft): bheda (division), dana (gifts) and sama (conciliation). Kautilya treats the same means at length. The last words, valla thamaichchu, are an older way of writing valladhu amaichchu (‘the minister is one capable of’), and all three sources agree on the text. Varadarasanar’s gloss and Kalaignar’s specify that those to be divided are the enemy’s helpers, which keeps the verse within fair statecraft rather than general intrigue.

tamil:
தெரிதலும் தேர்ந்து செயலும் ஒருதலையாச்
சொல்லலும் வல்லது அமைச்சு.
transliteration:
Theridhalum thaerndhu seyalum orudhalaiyaach
Sollalum valladhu amaichchu.
current_meaning: A minister can study a matter thoroughly, act only after careful choice, and state a firm, clear conclusion.
elementary_explanation: A good referee watches the play closely, thinks for a moment, and then makes a clear call. He does not say “maybe”. This kural says a good adviser looks carefully, chooses wisely, and then speaks clearly.
university_explanation: Three abilities are named. Theridhal is examining or understanding the matter. Thaerndhu seyal is acting after deliberate selection of means. Orudhalaiyaach sollal is speaking decisively (orudhalai, ‘one-sided’, i.e. unambiguous). Commentators differ on the last. Varadarasanar and Kesikan take it as boldness and clarity, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses asserting only what is beneficial. The Parimelazhagar tradition ties it to giving the king a settled opinion rather than a list of options, much as Kautilya’s teacher Pishuna asks for counsellors ‘capable of giving decisive opinion’. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read valladhu amaichu, and thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the older form ‘valla thamaichchu’. The two are the same words divided differently.

tamil:
அறனறிந்து ஆன்றமைந்த சொல்லான்எஞ் ஞான்றுந்
திறனறிந்தான் தேர்ச்சித் துணை.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu aandramaindha sollaan enjnjaandrum
Thiranarindhaan thaerchchith thunai.
current_meaning: The best partner in deliberation is one who knows what is right, speaks with full learning and restraint, and always knows how things are to be done.
elementary_explanation: When you need advice about something hard, you go to the person who knows right from wrong, speaks calmly and carefully, and knows the practical steps. This kural says that kind of person is the best helper for a leader.
university_explanation: The couplet sets out three qualifications for a thaerchchith thunai, a ‘companion in deliberation’. The first is aranarindhu, knowing aram (dharma or righteousness). The second is aandramaindha sollaan, one whose speech is full (aandru, ‘abundant, filled with learning’) and measured (amaindha, ‘settled, restrained’). The third is enjnjaandrum thiranarindhaan, one who always knows the method. Commentators differ over whether aandru points to learning, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take it, or to maturity. Pappaiah reads amaindha as modest or restrained speech. Parimelazhagar’s reading places moral knowledge first, so the counsellor’s skill serves aram rather than mere expediency. All three editions agree on the text; the older one divides it as ‘aranarindh aandramaindha sollaanenjnjaandrun’.

tamil:
மதிநுட்பம் நூலோடு உடையார்க்கு அதிநுட்பம்
யாவுள முன்நிற் பவை.
transliteration:
Madhinutpam noolodu udaiyaarkku adhinutpam
Yaavula munnir pavai.
current_meaning: What scheme, however subtle, can stand against someone who has natural sharpness of mind together with book learning?
elementary_explanation: Some kids are naturally quick at puzzles, and some have read lots of puzzle books. A kid who is both quick and well-read is very hard to trick. This kural says a good adviser is like that, so no clever trap can fool him.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts madhinutpam, native acuteness of intellect, with nool, learning from texts, and says that someone who has both cannot be outwitted by any adhinutpam, any ‘extreme subtlety’ or stratagem. The rhetorical question yaavula munnirpavai (‘what are there that stand before [him]?’) implies ‘none’. Commentators from Parimelazhagar on distinguish iyarkai arivu (natural intelligence) from seyarkai arivu (acquired or learned intelligence). This pair prepares for kural 637, which uses the same iyarkai and seyarkai vocabulary. Kalaignar and Pappaiah read adhinutpam specifically as hostile schemes (soozhchi). There are small spelling differences, such as முன்நிற் (ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net) against முன்னிற் and the joined ‘மதிநுட்ப நூலோ டுடையார்க்’ in the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org, but the wording is the same.

tamil:
செயற்கை அறிந்தக் கடைத்தும் உலகத்து
இயற்கை அறிந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Seyarkai arindhak kadaiththum ulakaththu
Iyarkai arindhu seyal.
current_meaning: Even when you know from books how a thing should be done, act only after understanding how the world actually works.
elementary_explanation: You can read a book about riding a bicycle, but you also need to notice the real road, the bumps and the traffic. This kural says that even after learning the rules, you must look at the real world and act in a way that fits it.
university_explanation: The couplet sets seyarkai, the ‘made’ or acquired knowledge of methods found in treatises, against ulakaththu iyarkai, the natural ways of the world. The minister should act (seyal) only after knowing the second as well as the first. Mu. Varadarasanar’s gloss makes seyarkai explicitly nool arivu (book knowledge). Solomon Pappaiah extends it to methods learned from foreign books and applies iyarkai to the character of one’s own land and people. Commentators in Parimelazhagar’s tradition often recall the grammarians’ rule that ulakam, ‘world’, can mean the worthy or experienced people whose conduct sets the norm. There is a small textual variant. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org read arindhak kadaiththum (with the doubled k), while thirukkural.net prints arindha kadaiththum. The meaning does not change.

tamil:
அறிகொன்று அறியான் எனினும் உறுதி
உழையிருந்தான் கூறல் கடன்.
transliteration:
Arikondru ariyaan eninum urudhi
Uzhaiyirundhaan kooral kadan.
current_meaning: Even if the king rejects wise advice and is ignorant himself, the one who stands beside him still has a duty to tell him what is truly good.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your friend is about to do something unsafe and will not listen. A true friend still tells them the truth, even if they get grumpy. This kural says a leader’s adviser must always tell the leader what is good, even when the leader does not want to hear it.
university_explanation: Arikondru (‘having killed knowledge’) is usually taken to mean that the king destroys or ignores the counsel of those who know. Ariyaan eninum (‘even if he himself does not know’) adds that he also lacks knowledge of his own. Even then urudhi (what is truly and lastingly beneficial) must be told (kooral kadan, ‘speaking is a duty’) by the uzhaiyirundhaan, ‘the one who is at his side’, meaning the minister. Solomon Pappaiah stresses that the minister must speak without anger and without fear. Kalaignar applies the verse to those near any ruler. The couplet is the moral centre of the chapter: the minister’s duty to give frank counsel does not depend on whether it will be welcomed. The thirukkural-thamizh.org edition prints ‘arikon rariyaa neninu murudhi / yuzhaiyirundhaan’, a difference of word division only.

tamil:
பழுதெண்ணும் மந்திரியின் பக்கததுள் தெவ்வோர்
எழுபது கோடி உறும்.
transliteration:
Pazhudhennum mandhiriyin pakkadhadhul thevvor
Ezhubadhu kodi urum.
current_meaning: Seventy crores of open enemies are better than one minister at your side who plots your ruin.
elementary_explanation: A lot of rivals on the other team are easier to handle than one teammate who is secretly trying to make you lose. This kural says a bad adviser close to a leader is more dangerous than a huge army of enemies.
university_explanation: Pazhudhennum mandhiri is ‘the minister who contemplates harm’. Mandhiri is from the Sanskrit mantrin; it stands beside the chapter’s Tamil amaichu. Pakkaththul means ‘at one’s side, within one’s own ranks’. Thevvor ezhubadhu kodi (seventy crores of enemies) is hyperbole for a countless host. There is a real textual and grammatical point here. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read mandhiriyin, while the older-orthography thirukkural-thamizh.org reads mandhiriyir (‘mandhiriyir pakkadhadhut tevvo’). Both are forms of the ablative of comparison, ‘than the minister’. That is why Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Kesikan read ‘seventy crore foes are better than such a minister’. Solomon Pappaiah reads it instead as ‘such a minister equals seventy crore foes’ and glosses pazhudhu as self-interest over the nation’s good.

tamil:
முறைப்படச் சூழ்ந்தும் முடிவிலவே செய்வர்
திறப்பாடு இலாஅ தவர்.
transliteration:
Muraippadach soozhndhum mudivilavae seyvar
Thirappaadu ilaaa thavar.
current_meaning: Those without the skill to carry things through will leave their work unfinished, even when they have planned it properly.
elementary_explanation: You can draw a perfect plan for a sandcastle, but if you do not know how to pack the sand, it falls apart halfway. This kural says a good plan is not enough; an adviser also needs the skill to finish the job.
university_explanation: Muraippadach soozhndhum means ‘even having deliberated in due order’, where soozhchi is the technical term for counsel. Such people mudivilavae seyvar, ‘do only things without completion’, if they are thirappaadu ilaadhavar, lacking executive ability. Ilaaa carries a prosodic lengthening (alapedai) needed for the metre. The thirukkural-thamizh.org edition prints ‘thirappaa delaaa thavar’, the older joined spelling of thirappaadu + ilaaa. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take mudivila to mean half-done or defective work, while Kesikan reads it as ‘endless’, never-concluding activity. Closing the chapter this way balances its stress on deliberation. Counsel without execution fails, which leads into the later chapters on action (vinaiththooimai, vinaiththitpam, vinaiseyalvagai, 66-68).

tamil:
நாநலம் என்னும் நலனுடைமை அந்நலம்
யாநலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
transliteration:
Naanalam ennum nalanudaimai annalam
Yaanalaththu ulladhooum andru.
current_meaning: The gift called goodness of the tongue is a wealth in its own right; it is not merely one item among the other good things a person may possess.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a treasure box holding gold, toys and books. A kind, clear way of speaking is not just one more thing in the box; it is like a special key that opens many other boxes. This kural says being able to speak well is a treasure all by itself.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the minister’s second great qualification after the preceding chapter on the minister (அமைச்சு, ch. 64): nā-nalam, literally “tongue-goodness”, is framed as a nalan-uṭaimai, a possession or wealth in the same grammatical mould as kalvi-uṭaimai or aṟivu-uṭaimai elsewhere in the text. The second line, yā-nalattu uḷḷatūum anṟu, says this good is “not contained within any other good”; the lengthened form uḷḷatūum is an alapeṭai (metrical prolongation). Parimelazhagar explains that eloquence is a distinct excellence because the other goods of a minister (lineage, learning, wealth) cannot be made effective in council without it, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading of it as a unique, self-standing merit. Some later commentators, including Kalaignar, read the line more strongly as “the best of all wealth”, a slight shift from “not included among” to “superior to” the other goods. The text is stable across ytamizh.com and the older sandhi-joined edition at thirukkural-thamizh.org (நாநல மென்னு நலனுடைமை யந்நலம்).

tamil:
ஆக்கமுங் கேடும் அதனால் வருதலால்
காத்தோம்பல் சொல்லின்கட் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Aakkamung kedum adhanaal varudhalaal
Kaaththombal sollinkat sorvu.
current_meaning: Since both prosperity and ruin come through speech, a person must guard carefully against any slip in what they say.
elementary_explanation: Words are like the steering wheel of a car: turn it well and you get home safely, jerk it carelessly and you crash. Because words can build things up or break them down, we should be careful never to say the wrong thing.
university_explanation: Ākkam (growth, prosperity) and kēṭu (ruin) are the paired outcomes that Valluvar often sets against each other, and here both are said to arrive “by it” (atanāl), meaning speech. The verb phrase kāttu ōmpal, “guarding and protecting”, is a doubled imperative of care, and cōrvu names a lapse, slip or momentary negligence, not deliberate lying. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as advice to the minister, whose words in council can raise or ruin the king’s affairs, and so the lapse to be guarded against is any fault in word choice or timing. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar) widen it into a universal maxim of verbal care. The older edition prints the first line in sandhi form (ஆக்கமுங் கேடு மதனால் வருதலாற்), with no difference in meaning.

tamil:
கேட்டார்ப் பிணிக்கும் தகையவாய்க் கேளாரும்
வேட்ப மொழிவதாம் சொல்.
transliteration:
Kettaarp pinikkum thakaiyavaaik kelaarum
Vetpa mozhivadhaam sol.
current_meaning: True eloquence holds those who hear it as if bound, and is spoken so well that even those who have not heard it long to hear it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a storyteller so good that the children listening can’t look away, and children walking past stop and want to join in. That is what this kural calls real speaking skill.
university_explanation: The key verb piṇittal means to bind or tie (as with a rope), so the listener is pictured as captured by the speech, and vēṭpa means “so as to make them desire”. The contrast kēṭṭār / kēḷār, “those who have heard / those who have not heard”, is read two ways. Parimelazhagar takes kēṭṭār as allies or friends (those already listening) and kēḷār as enemies or those who refuse to listen; this is why Pope’s gloss speaks of binding friends and making even enemies desire. Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading but also records the plainer sense of those who heard before and those who have not yet heard. The couplet is effectively the chapter’s definition of sol-vanmai, ending emphatically with -ām col, “that is speech”.

tamil:
திறனறிந்து சொல்லுக சொல்லை அறனும்
பொருளும் அதனினூஉங்கு இல்.
transliteration:
Thiranarindhu solluka sollai aranum
Porulum adhaninoongu il.
current_meaning: Speak only after understanding the nature of your listeners; there is no virtue or gain greater than speech fitted to its hearers.
elementary_explanation: You explain a game differently to your little cousin than to your teacher. This kural says the smart thing is to know who is listening and choose your words for them, and that doing this is one of the best things you can do.
university_explanation: Tiṟan aṟintu, “knowing the tiṟan”, is the interpretive crux. Parimelazhagar takes tiṟan as the qualities of the audience, and Solomon Pappaiah lists them: birth, learning, conduct, wealth, appearance and age. Mu. Varadarasanar reads tiṟan as the right manner or force of the words themselves, and Kalaignar as the underlying reason for speaking. The second line makes a striking claim with the comparative atanin ūungu, “beyond that”, lengthened for metre: neither aṟam (virtue, the first puruṣārtha) nor poruḷ (wealth, the second) exceeds well-fitted speech. The claim makes sense within Porutpal, where the minister’s speech is the means by which both dharma and wealth are secured for the kingdom.

tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லைப் பிறிதோர்சொல் அச்சொல்லை
வெல்லுஞ்சொல் இன்மை அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Solluka sollaip pirithorsol achchollai
Vellunjol inmai arindhu.
current_meaning: Speak your word only after making sure there is no other word that could defeat it.
elementary_explanation: Before you give your answer in a debate, check it from every side, like testing a bridge before you walk on it. If nobody can knock it down, then say it.
university_explanation: The couplet is famous for its sound play: col (word) appears five times in two lines, in collu-ka, collai, piṟitōr col, accollai and vellum col, so the verse enacts the verbal skill it recommends. The sense is that before speaking one should know (aṟintu) that no other word (piṟitu ōr col) that would overcome (vellum) that word exists (inmai). Parimelazhagar applies this to the minister in council, whose proposal must be answer-proof before it is offered to the king; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say the same. The older edition shows sandhi forms (பிறிதோர்சொ லச்சொல்லை / வெல்லுஞ்சொ லின்மை யறிந்து), with no difference in meaning.

tamil:
வேட்பத்தாஞ் சொல்லிப் பிறர்சொல் பயன்கோடல்
மாட்சியின் மாசற்றார் கோள்.
transliteration:
Vetpaththaanj sollip pirarsol payankodal
Maatchiyin maasatraar kol.
current_meaning: To speak so that others long to hear, and to take the useful meaning from what others say, is the practice of people of flawless excellence.
elementary_explanation: A good friend talks in a way you enjoy hearing, and when you talk, they listen for what you really mean instead of picking on small mistakes. This kural says the best people do both: speak well and listen well.
university_explanation: The couplet balances two actions: vēṭpat tām colli (oneself speaking so as to be desired) and piṟar col payan kōṭal (taking the payan, the fruit or meaning, of others’ words). Parimelazhagar adds that in hearing others one should grasp the substance while overlooking faults in their wording, and Solomon Pappaiah follows him. Māṭciyin mācaṟṟār, “those without stain in their excellence”, and kōḷ, “principle or settled practice”, present this as the rule of the most accomplished counsellors. It widens sol-vanmai from speaking to include skilled listening. The older edition reads பிறர்சொற் பயன்கோடன் in sandhi form.

tamil:
சொலல்வல்லன் சோர்விலன் அஞ்சான் அவனை
இகல்வெல்லல் யார்க்கும் அரிது.
transliteration:
Solalvallan sorvilan anjaan avanai
Ikalvellal yaarkkum aridhu.
current_meaning: No one can easily overcome in contest a person who speaks with power, never slips, and does not fear.
elementary_explanation: Picture a class debate. The student who explains clearly, doesn’t forget their points, and isn’t scared to speak up is very hard to beat. This kural says those three things together make someone almost unbeatable.
university_explanation: Three predicate nouns build the ideal speaker: colal vallan (strong in speaking), cōrvilan (without lapse; Parimelazhagar glosses cōrvu as forgetfulness of what is to be said, echoing 642) and añcān (one who does not fear, above all fear of the assembly, the theme of chapter 73, Avaiyañcāmai). Ikal means enmity, rivalry or contention, so ikal vellal is victory through opposition; Pope renders it as intrigue or “hostile power”. Solomon Pappaiah expands the three terms to the ability to make others accept one’s thought, persistence even when the message is hard, and fearlessness even before hostile hearers. The older edition prints சோர்வில னஞ்சா னவனை / யிகல்வெல்லல் in sandhi form.

tamil:
விரைந்து தொழில்கேட்கும் ஞாலம் நிரந்தினிது
சொல்லுதல் வல்லார்ப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Viraindhu thozhilkekkum gnaalam nirandhinidhu
Solludhal vallaarp perin.
current_meaning: If the world finds people who can speak in good order and pleasantly, it will quickly do what they ask.
elementary_explanation: If a coach explains the plan step by step and in a friendly way, the whole team gets moving straight away. This kural says people are happy to follow someone whose words are clear, well arranged and kind.
university_explanation: Nirantu, “in proper sequence, arranged in order”, is the key technical term: it describes dispositio, the arrangement of points in the right order, joined with initu, pleasantly. Toḻil kēṭkum ñālam, “the world that hears or obeys the command”, uses kēḷ in the sense of obedience, and viraintu (swiftly) stresses how quickly the result follows. Parimelazhagar reads ñālam as the people of the world and the couplet as describing the minister whose orderly, sweet speech gets the king’s business done at once. Pope’s rendering, the world gathering round, softens the sense of obedience. The older edition prints கேட்கு ஞால நிரந்தினிது.

tamil:
பலசொல்லக் காமுறுவர் மன்றமா சற்ற
சிலசொல்லல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Palasollak kaamuruvar mandramaa satra
Silasollal thetraa thavar.
current_meaning: Those who do not know how to say a few flawless words are surely the ones who love to say many.
elementary_explanation: Some people talk and talk because they can’t find the right few words. Someone who knows exactly what to say can say it quickly and clearly, like a good arrow that hits the target in one shot.
university_explanation: The couplet sets pala (many) against cila (few), and māc aṟṟa (stainless, faultless) qualifies the few words. Kāmuṟuvar, “they desire”, turns wordiness into a craving. Maṉṟa is an emphatic particle, “certainly, surely”, which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as uṇmaiyāka. Tēṟṟātavar means those who are not able or not skilled: Parimelazhagar takes it as inability to express a matter in few faultless words, so wordiness is a symptom of lacking the skill, not a separate vice. Pope’s rendering (“Who have not skill ten faultless words to utter plain”) adds a number not in the Tamil. In the older edition the second line reads சிலசொல்ல றேற்றா தவர், where sandhi turns collal tēṟṟā into colla ṟēṟṟā.

tamil:
இணருழ்த்தும் நாறா மலரனையர் கற்றது
உணர விரித்துரையா தார்.
transliteration:
Inaroozhththum naaraa malaranaiyar katradhu
Unara viriththuraiyaa thaar.
current_meaning: Those who cannot explain what they have learned so that others understand it are like flowers that bloom in clusters but give no fragrance.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a bunch of beautiful flowers that have no smell at all: nice to look at, but something is missing. A person who knows a lot but can’t explain it to anyone is like that. Learning is meant to be shared.
university_explanation: The closing couplet uses an uvamai (simile): iṇar (a cluster or bunch) ūḻttum (though it blossoms) nāṟā malar (a flower that gives no scent). Kaṟṟatu uṇara virittu uraiyātār means those who do not expand (virittu) and state (urai) what they have learned so that others may grasp it (uṇara). Parimelazhagar’s point is that learning (kalvi), however full, is incomplete in a counsellor unless it can be communicated, which links this chapter back to ch. 40 (Kalvi) and ch. 42 (Kēḷvi). The texts differ on the first word: ytamizh.com prints இணருழ்த்தும் with a short u, and the older edition prints இணருழ்த்து நாறா; many standard editions have the expected long-vowel form இணரூழ்த்தும் (iṇar + ūḻttum). The older edition also divides the second line as கற்ற / துணர விரித்துரையா தார் for metre.

tamil:
துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம்
வேண்டிய எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Thunainalam aakkam tharooum vinainalam
Vendiya ellaan tharum.
current_meaning: Good allies can bring a person increase and wealth, but goodness in the deeds themselves brings everything one could wish for.
elementary_explanation: Good friends can help you build a bigger sandcastle. But if you build it the right way, patiently and fairly, you get the castle, you keep your friends, and people want to play with you again. Doing things the right way gives you more than any helper can.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by ranking two kinds of nalam (goodness, excellence): tuṇai-nalam, the excellence of one’s supporters, the theme of the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (ch. 45), and vinai-nalam, the goodness or purity of the action itself, which gives the chapter its name, vinai-t-tūymai. Parimelazhagar reads ākkam narrowly as material increase, while vēṇṭiya ellām (all that is desired) takes in fame and merit in this world and the next, so good allies secure only one good while pure action secures all of them. The line sets the ethical frame for this part of the Amaichiyal (chapters on the minister, 64-73): a minister’s competence (ch. 64) and eloquence (ch. 65) are worthless unless the means he uses are clean. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this contrast closely, while Kalaignar softens it into a partnership in which allies add strength and good deeds done with them bring every benefit. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both print த்ருஉம், an evident keying error. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org has தரூஉம் (tarūum, the alapeṭai lengthening of tarum), and that reading is adopted here.

tamil:
என்றும் ஒருவுதல் வேண்டும் புகழொடு
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
transliteration:
Endrum oruvudhal vendum pugazhodu
Nandri payavaa vinai.
current_meaning: At all times one must give up any deed that brings neither honour nor real good.
elementary_explanation: Before you do something, ask two questions: will people be proud of me for this, and will it truly help? If the answer to both is no, don’t do it, even if it looks easy or tempting.
university_explanation: The couplet gives the test that runs through the whole chapter: a deed must yield pukaḻ (fame, good name) together with naṉṟi (benefit, goodness), and a deed that yields neither is to be avoided (oruvutal, ‘setting aside, shunning’) at all times (eṉṟum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah read the pair as fame in this life and merit (aṟam) for the life to come, so a clean act must be both publicly honourable and morally fruitful. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the rejected deeds as those ‘without purity’ (tūymai aṟṟa), tying the verse to the chapter title. The prose explanation printed with Pope’s translation (‘acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit’) reads pukaḻoṭu slightly differently, but all readings agree that honour alone is not enough without real good. The text is stable across all three sources consulted.

tamil:
ஒஓதல் வேண்டும் ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை
ஆஅதும் என்னு மவர்.
transliteration:
Oodhal vendum olimaazhkum seyvinai
Aaadhum ennu mavar.
current_meaning: Those who say ‘we shall rise higher’ must avoid any deed that would dim the light of their good name.
elementary_explanation: If you want to become class captain, you wouldn’t cheat on a test, because once people see you cheat they stop trusting you. Anyone who wants to grow greater has to keep their good name bright and stay away from anything that would spoil it.
university_explanation: Two alapeṭai (metrical lengthenings) mark the couplet: ஒஓதல் for ஓதல்/ஒருவுதல் (avoiding, shunning), and ஆஅதும் for ஆதும், ‘we shall become (greater)’, which Parimelazhagar takes as the resolve of those who seek to rise ever higher. Oḷi (light, radiance) stands here for reputation and dignity, and oḷi-māḻkum seyviṉai means acts that cause that radiance to fade. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both take oḷi as pukaḻ (fame), linking this verse to the fame-and-good test of 652, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as ‘one’s standing in one’s own lifetime’. The logic is a statesman’s: ambition itself is a reason for scruple, since a stained name blocks the rise one hopes for. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined form ஒஓதல் வேண்டு மொளிமாழ்குஞ் செய்வினை / யாஅது மென்னு மவர்.

tamil:
இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார்
நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Idukkan padinum ilivandha seyyaar
Nadukkatra kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: People of clear, unshaken understanding will not do anything shameful, even when they are in serious trouble.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you lost your lunch money and saw someone else’s wallet on the floor. A person with a steady, clear mind would still hand it in, even though they’re hungry. Being in trouble doesn’t make a wrong thing right.
university_explanation: Iṭukkaṇ is ‘distress, affliction’ (compare the chapter iṭukkaṇ aḻiyāmai, ch. 63), and iḷivanta means ‘what brings disgrace’. Parimelazhagar takes the past-tense participle literally as ‘acts that have (in the past) brought disgrace’, which is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)’. The key phrase naṭukku-aṟṟa kāṭci, ‘vision free of trembling’, describes firm, clear discernment that does not waver under pressure, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘motionless, clear knowledge’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar add that such people will not act basely even to escape their distress, which prepares for the stronger case of 656. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read இடுக்கண் படினும்; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi form இடுக்கட் படினு மிளிவந்த.

tamil:
எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க செய்வானேல்
மற்றன்ன செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Etrendru iranguva seyyarka seyvaanel
Matranna seyyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Do nothing that will later make you cry ‘What have I done!’; and if you have done such a thing, it is good not to do the like again.
elementary_explanation: If you ever do something that makes you think ‘Oh no, why did I do that?’, the best thing is to learn from it and never do it again. Even better is to stop and think first, so you don’t have to feel that way at all.
university_explanation: Eṟṟu eṉṟu is an exclamation of dismay (‘what is this!’), and iraṅkuva are deeds one will afterwards lament. The first line forbids such deeds, and the second deals with the case where one has already done one. Here the commentaries split. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read maṟṟu aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing such things again’, so repentance means not repeating the fault. The older reading, kept in the Drew-Lazarus prose explanation printed with Pope (‘it were good that he grieved not’) and in Puliyur Kesikan, takes aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing that (grieving) again’: a minister should not waste himself in useless regret. This reading is usually traced to Parimelazhagar. The text also varies: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read செய்வானேல் (‘if he does’), while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints செய்வானேன், probably a typographical variant, since the conditional -ēl is needed for the sense.

tamil:
ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினுஞ் செய்யற்க
சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை.
transliteration:
Eendraal pasikaanbaan aayinum seyyarka
Saandror pazhikkum vinai.
current_meaning: Even if you must watch your own mother go hungry, do not do what the wise condemn.
elementary_explanation: Suppose someone you love very much needs help. You would want to do anything for them, but stealing or lying still isn’t the right way. The Kural says even love for your own mother doesn’t make a wrong deed right. You must find an honest way to help.
university_explanation: This is the strongest statement in the chapter. Īṉṟāḷ, ‘she who bore (you)’, is the mother; pacikāṇpāṉ āyiṉum means ‘even if he should (have to) see her hunger’. Tamil ethics counts care of parents among the highest duties, so the verse deliberately picks the hardest case: not even that duty justifies deeds the cāṉṟōr (people of perfected character) condemn. Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators read the line without exception clauses, and Kalaignar sharpens it to ‘not even to relieve’ her suffering. This contrasts with the Sanskrit doctrine of āpad-dharma (law in emergencies), where the Mahabharata allows the sage Vishvamitra, in famine, to steal dog’s flesh to survive. The Kural here refuses that concession. The text is identical across sources apart from the sandhi form பசிகாண்பா னாயினுஞ் in thirukkural-thamizh.org. (Solomon Pappaiah’s printed gloss has பெற்றவனின், apparently a slip for பெற்றவளின்.)

tamil:
பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் சான்றோர்
கழிநல் குரவே தலை.
transliteration:
Pazhimalaindhu eydhiya aakkaththin saandror
Kazhinal kuravae thalai.
current_meaning: The deepest poverty of good people is better than wealth gained by taking on disgrace.
elementary_explanation: Would you rather have a small lunch you paid for honestly, or a big feast you got by cheating? The Kural says the small honest lunch is worth far more, because you can enjoy it with a clear heart.
university_explanation: Paḻi malaintu, ‘having taken on / worn blame’ (malai- as in wearing a garland), describes wealth won by accepting disgrace, and ākkattiṉ is the comparative ablative, ‘than such wealth’. Kaḻi nalkuravu is ‘extreme, excessive poverty’ (kaḻi = beyond measure). Parimelazhagar takes it as the poverty of the cāṉṟōr, and Mu. Varadarasanar adds that they accept it because they keep purity of action (viṉait-tūymai). Talai means ‘head, foremost’, so such poverty ranks first. The couplet restates 656 as a general value judgement and prepares for the fate of tainted wealth in 658-660. All three sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi forms மலைந் தெய்திய வாக்கத்திற்.

tamil:
கடிந்த கடிந்தொரார் செய்தார்க்கு அவைதாம்
முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்.
transliteration:
Kadindha kadindhoraar seydhaarkku avaidhaam
Mudindhaalum peezhai tharum.
current_meaning: For those who do what the wise have forbidden instead of avoiding it, those deeds bring suffering even when they succeed.
elementary_explanation: If you sneak a cookie from the jar after being told not to, you might get the cookie, but then you feel worried and guilty, and you might get caught later. Even when a wrong plan ‘works’, it ends up making you unhappy.
university_explanation: The first line plays on the verb kaṭi- (‘forbid, reject’): kaṭinta, ‘things forbidden (by the great)’, and kaṭintu orār, ‘those who do not reject them and turn away’. Solomon Pappaiah specifies that such people act ‘thinking to gather wealth’, keeping the chapter’s focus on means of gain. The concessive muṭintālum, ‘even if they are accomplished’, is the point: success does not clean a forbidden act, which still brings pīḻai (suffering, affliction). Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes the suffering to come in this life as well as the next, through loss of reputation and later retribution. All sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org divides it as செய்தார்க் கவைதா / முடிந்தாலும்.

tamil:
அழக்கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம் இழப்பினும்
பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பா லவை.
transliteration:
Azhakkonda ellaam azhappoam izhappinum
Pirpayakkum narpaa lavai.
current_meaning: All that is taken by making others weep will go away and leave the taker weeping; what is gained by good means, even if lost for a while, bears fruit later.
