The superlative nandrendravatrullum nandre (good even among the things called good) is strong praise: such restraint is ranked above other virtues of the counsellor. Kalaignar’s paraphrase adds a vivid Tamil idiom, “like a cashew seed” (mundhiri kottai), for a person who pushes forward to speak. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “நன்றென்ற வற்றுள்ளு நன்றே முதுவருண்”.

chapter_title: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
tamil:
ஆற்றின் நிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புலம்
ஏற்றுணர்வார் முன்னர் இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Aatrin nilaithalarndh thatre viyanpulam
Etrunarvaar munnar izhukku.
current_meaning: To slip up in speech before people who have taken in and understood vast fields of learning is like losing your footing and falling from the path.
elementary_explanation: A spelling mistake in a note to your friend is no big deal. The same mistake in the final round of a spelling bee, in front of the judges, feels like tripping on stage. Mistakes count most in front of experts.
university_explanation: Viyanpulam (wide fields, meaning vast areas of learning) etrunarvaar (those who have received and understood them) are the most demanding audience there is, and an izhukku (slip or lapse) before them is compared to aatrin nilaithalarndhatru, losing one’s footing on the way. Commentators disagree about aaru. Parimelazhagar and most modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take it as the path of right conduct, so a verbal slip before the learned is as disgraceful as a good man’s moral lapse. Puliyur Kesikan takes aaru as a river and reads the image as a swimmer losing his footing mid-stream, so the lapse is dangerous and hard to recover from. The kural thus explains why 715’s restraint matters: before the learned the cost of error is very high. The text agrees in all sources; the sandhi text reads “ஆற்றி னிலைதளர்ந் தற்றே வியன்புல மேற்றுணர்வார் முன்ன ரிழுக்கு”.

chapter_title: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
tamil:
கற்றறிந்தார் கல்வி விளங்கும் கசடறச்
சொல்தெரிதல் வல்லார் அகத்து.
transliteration:
Katrarindhaar kalvi vilangum kasadarach
Soltheridhal vallaar akaththu.
current_meaning: The learning of those who have studied deeply shines most brightly among people who can judge words flawlessly.
elementary_explanation: A great chess move looks like nothing special to someone who doesn’t know chess. Show it to a chess champion and they gasp, “Wow!” Your best work shines most in front of people who can understand it.
university_explanation: Vilangum (will shine, become manifest) is the key verb. Learning does not show its worth in a vacuum. It becomes visible only in the akam (midst, company) of those who are kasadara soltheridhal vallaar, able to examine words kasadara, without flaw or dross. Kasadu (impurity, dross) links back to Valluvar’s famous command in ch. 40, Kalvi (kural 391): “கற்க கசடறக் கற்பவை.” There is a pairing here: flawless study (391) meets flawless hearing (717). Commentators note that this kural balances 716. The expert audience that punishes a slip is also the only audience that can properly recognise real learning. The ytamizh/thirukkural.net text “சொல்தெரிதல்” and the sandhi form “சொற்றெரிதல்” are the same word.

chapter_title: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
tamil:
உணர்வ துடையார்முன் சொல்லல் வளர்வதன்
பாத்தியுள் நீர்சொரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Unarva thudaiyaarmun sollal valarvadhan
Paaththiyul neersorindh thatru.
current_meaning: Speaking before people who can understand is like pouring water into a garden bed where plants are already growing.
elementary_explanation: Watering a plant that is already sprouting makes it shoot up fast. Watering an empty patch of dirt does nothing. Telling good ideas to someone who wants to learn is like watering the sprout.
university_explanation: This kural is the positive counterpart of the chapter’s closing image (720). Unarvadhu udaiyaar are people who have understanding, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah stress that they understand for themselves (thaame unargindra), even without being told. Speaking to them is like watering (neer sorindhatru) a paaththi, a small irrigated garden bed, in which the crop is valarvadhu, already growing of its own accord. The image is agricultural and exact: the water does not create growth but speeds up growth that is already under way, so the speaker’s words bear fruit at once. Parimelazhagar takes this as the assembly of equals in learning, and so completes the scheme begun in 714. The text agrees across sources; the sandhi text reads “உணர்வ துடையார்முற் சொல்லல்” and “பாத்தியு ணீர்சொரிந் தற்று”.

chapter_title: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
tamil:
புல்லவையுள் பொச்சாந்தும் சொல்லற்க நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
transliteration:
Pullavaiyul pochchaandhum sollarka nallavaiyul
Nanku selach chollu vaar.
current_meaning: Those who can speak good things persuasively in a worthy assembly should never, even by forgetting themselves, speak them in a mean one.
elementary_explanation: You wouldn’t show your best drawing to kids who you know will just scribble on it and laugh. Save it for people who will really look at it. Good words should be shared with good listeners.
university_explanation: Pullavai (a low or mean assembly, from pul, grass, meaning petty or base) is set against nallavai (a good assembly). Pochchaandhum (even through forgetfulness) uses the root of ch. 54, Pochchaavaamai (Unforgetfulness): the speaker is not to slip, even for a moment, into speaking before an unworthy audience. Nanku sela sollu (to speak so that it goes in well) describes speech that enters and settles in the hearers’ minds. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as speech that is “fixed in the mind” (manadhil padhiyumaaru). The ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net texts print “நன்குசலச்”, apparently a corruption. The sandhi text “நன்கு செலச்சொல்லு வார்” and P. A. Muthukrishnan’s musical setting (“நன்கு செலச் சொல்லுவார்”, quoted on thirukkural.net) support the reading செல, which Parimelazhagar’s gloss (to cause to enter) also requires.

chapter_title: The Knowledge of the Council Chamber
tamil:
அங்கணத்துள் உக்க அமிழ்தற்றால் தங்கணத்தார்
அல்லார்முன் கோட்டி கொளல்.
transliteration:
Anganaththul ukka amizhdhatraal thanganaththaar
Allaarmun kotti kolal.
current_meaning: Holding forth before people who are not of one’s own kind is like nectar spilled into a gutter.
elementary_explanation: Imagine pouring the most delicious juice in the world down the drain. What a waste! Explaining something wonderful to people who don’t care at all is like that. The juice was good; it just went to the wrong place.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with its most memorable image. Amizhdhu (amrita, the nectar of immortality) is ukka (spilled) into an anganam, the drain of a house’s open courtyard: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss it as an unclean courtyard, Solomon Pappaiah as a sewer. Thanganaththaar allaar are those who are not of one’s own gana (group, circle), meaning not one’s equals in learning and outlook. Kotti kolal (to hold a discourse) uses kotti, cognate with Sanskrit goshthi (assembly, learned conversation). The simile, like 718’s, is exact. Nectar is not spoiled by being spilled, but it can never be recovered or drunk, so it is wasted. The sources differ slightly on one form: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read தங்கணத்தார், while the sandhi-joined text reads “தங்கணத்த ரல்லார்முற்” (தங்கணத்தர்). The meaning is unaffected.

tamil:
வகையறிந்து வல்லவை வாய்சோரார் சொல்லின்
தொகையறிந்த தூய்மை யவர்.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarindhu vallavai vaaisoraar sollin
Thokaiyarindha thooimai yavar.
current_meaning: People of pure mind who know the full range of words, and who first size up what kind of assembly they are facing, will not stumble in their speech before a powerful gathering.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you know every line of the school play, and you have peeked out to see who is in the audience. Because you know your words and you know who is listening, your voice stays steady. Knowing your words and knowing your listeners keeps you from getting tongue-tied.
university_explanation: This couplet opens Avaiyañcāmai (“not fearing the assembly”). It pairs with the chapter before it, Avaiyaṟital (knowing the assembly), inside the Amaicciyal, the section on ministers. Parimelazhagar reads vakai aṟintu (“knowing the kind”) as first working out what sort of assembly one is in. Vallavai is the assembly of the able or powerful, and vāy sōrār means “their mouths will not slip,” that is, they will not falter or make mistakes out of fear. Sollin tokai aṟinda tūymaiyavar are “the pure who know the tokai (range or classification) of words,” which commentators connect with a grammarian’s knowledge of word-classes and how to use them. So the chapter’s first answer to stage fright is skill combined with integrity. The sandhi-joined text reads “சொல்லின் றொகையறிந்த,” where றொ is simply ன் fused with தொ, and the words are unchanged.

tamil:
கற்றாருள் கற்றார் எனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முன்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லு வார்.
transliteration:
Katraarul katraar enappaduvar katraarmun
Katra selachchollu vaar.
current_meaning: Those who can set out what they have learned before learned people, in a way that actually reaches them, are called the most learned of the learned.
elementary_explanation: Lots of kids can read a book. The one who can explain it clearly to the whole class, even with the teacher listening, is the one everyone calls the real expert.
university_explanation: The line repeats kaṟṟār (“the learned”) four times. The word-play mirrors the idea that learning is measured among the learned. The key term is cela-c-colluvār, “those who speak so that it goes (cel-)” into the hearers. Parimelazhagar glosses it as speaking so that the matter enters the listeners’ minds, and Mu. Varadarasanar likewise says “so that it settles in their hearts.” The judgement is about rank: standing among scholars comes from being able to explain things well before one’s peers, not from private learning. The sandhi-joined text reads “கற்றாருட் கற்றா ரெனப்படுவர் கற்றார்முற்,” in which ட் and ற் are sound-changes of ள் and ன் before க.

tamil:
பகையகத்துச் சாவார் எளியர் அரியர்
அவையகத்து அஞ்சா தவர்.
transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththuch chaavaar eliyar ariyar
Avaiyakaththu anjaa thavar.
current_meaning: People willing to die in the midst of enemies are easy to find. People who stand in an assembly without fear are rare.
elementary_explanation: Lots of people are brave in a game or on the playground. Standing up in front of the whole school to say what you really think takes a different kind of courage, and fewer people have it.
university_explanation: The couplet is built as a sharp contrast: pakai-y-akattu (“inside the enemy ranks”) against avai-y-akattu (“inside the assembly”), and eḷiyar (“easy to find, many”) against ariyar (“rare”). Parimelazhagar takes the first group as warriors who throw themselves fearlessly among the enemy and die, and the second as those who are unafraid before the learned. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the first as “many in the world.” The couplet ranks civil courage above martial courage, a bold claim in a culture whose puṟam poetry celebrated heroic death. The sandhi-joined text “பகையகத்துச் சாவா ரெளிய ரரிய / ரவையகத் தஞ்சா தவர்” divides into the same words.

tamil:
கற்றார்முன் கற்ற செலச்சொல்லித் தாம்கற்ற
மிக்காருள் மிக்க கொளல்.
transliteration:
Katraarmun katra selachchollith thaamkatra
Mikkaarul mikka kolal.
current_meaning: Present what you have learned before the learned so that it reaches them, and then take from those who know more whatever goes beyond your own knowledge.
elementary_explanation: Share what you know in class. Then listen to the teacher and the older kids who know even more. Speaking up and listening both help you grow.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats the formula kaṟṟār mun kaṟṟa cela-c-colli from 722 and adds a second duty: mikkāruḷ mikka koḷal, “take the surplus from those who surpass you.” Parimelazhagar reads mikkār as those superior in learning and mikka as whatever their learning holds beyond one’s own. The ytamizh commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree. Speaking before the learned is therefore not a performance but one part of a cycle of learning: speak, be tested, learn more. The sandhi-joined text has “தாங்கற்ற” and “மிக்காருண்” for தாம்கற்ற and மிக்காருள்.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து கற்க அவையஞ்சா
மாற்றங் கொடுத்தற் பொருட்டு.
transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu karka avaiyanjaa
Maatrang koduththar poruttu.
current_meaning: Study the proper method of reasoning, by the rules, so that you can give answers in an assembly without fear.
elementary_explanation: If you want to answer tricky questions without getting nervous, practise thinking things through step by step. When you know how to reason, a hard question doesn’t scare you.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar reads āṟṟin aḷavu aṟintu kaṟka as “learn, by the proper path (of grammar), the aḷavai-nūl,” that is, the science of pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge), or logic. Solomon Pappaiah paraphrases it as tarka śāstra, the logic of proofs, and Kalaignar as grammar together with logic. Māṟṟam koṭuttal means “giving a reply,” so the purpose of this study is avai añcā, not fearing the assembly, above all when being cross-questioned. Some modern readers take āṟṟin aḷavu more loosely as “the measure of one’s ability” or “the scope of the subject.” The sandhi text “ஆற்றின் னளவறிந்து” shows a metrical doubling, and the words are the same.

tamil:
வாளொடென் வன்கண்ணர் அல்லார்க்கு நூலொடென்
நுண்ணவை அஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Vaalodden vankannar allaarkku noolodden
Nunnavai anju pavarkku.
current_meaning: What use is a sword to someone without courage? What use are books to someone who is afraid of an assembly of sharp minds?
elementary_explanation: A shiny sword is no use to a knight who runs away. In the same way, knowing lots of facts doesn’t help if you’re too scared ever to say them.
university_explanation: Two parallel questions, vāḷoṭu eṉ (“what [has he] to do with a sword?”) and nūloṭu eṉ (“what with books?”), set weapons and learning side by side. Vaṉkaṇ, literally “hard eye,” means steady courage. Nuṇ-avai is an assembly of subtle, sharp minds. Solomon Pappaiah takes nūl specifically as books of logic, continuing from 725, while Kalaignar reads it broadly as learning in general. On all readings the logic is the same: just as a sword is useful only to the brave, learning is useful only to someone who can use it before the learned. Owning it without using it is the same as not owning it. The sandhi text reads “வன்கண்ண ரல்லார்க்கு நூலொடெ / னுண்ணவை யஞ்சு பவர்க்கு.”

tamil:
பகையகத்துப் பேடிகை ஒள்வாள் அவையகத்து
அஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.
transliteration:
Pakaiyakaththup pedikai olvaal avaiyakaththu
Anju mavankatra nool.
current_meaning: The learning of someone who is afraid in the assembly is like a gleaming sword in the hand of a man unfit to fight, facing the enemy: sharp, but never used.
elementary_explanation: Picture a very sharp, shiny sword held by someone who is shaking too hard to lift it. It looks impressive but does nothing. Learning you’re too scared to share is just like that sword.
university_explanation: This couplet turns 726 into a single simile: pēṭi kai oḷ vāḷ, “the bright sword in the hand of a pēṭi.” In classical Tamil, pēṭi means a person who is neither man nor woman, traditionally glossed as a eunuch or hermaphrodite. Pope and Drew translate it “hermaphrodite,” and Pope’s verse has “sexless being.” The martial culture of the time used such a person as a stock figure for someone unfit for battle; the image reflects that period’s assumptions, not a judgement the modern reader needs to share. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all stress uselessness: the sword is fine, but the hand fails it. The couplet also repeats 723’s pakai-y-akattu / avai-y-akattu frame. The sandhi text reads “பேடிகை யொள்வா ளவையகத் / தஞ்சு மவன்கற்ற நூல்.”

tamil:
பல்லவை கற்றும் பயமிலரே நல்லவையுள்
நன்கு செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
transliteration:
Pallavai katrum payamilare nallavaiyul
Nanku selachchollaa thaar.
current_meaning: However many subjects they have studied, people who cannot put good things well and persuasively before a good assembly are of no use.
elementary_explanation: A treasure chest that stays locked forever is no better than an empty box. If you learn lots of things but never share them clearly, nobody gets any good out of them.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on the syllable avai: pal-l-avai (“many things”) and nal-l-avai (“a good assembly”) echo each other. Payam ilar means “without benefit.” Here payam is the classical form of payaṉ (use, fruit), not the modern Tamil word for fear, a false friend worth pointing out in a chapter about fear. Nalla avai is the assembly of good or learned people, and naṉku cela-c-collutal again means speech that reaches and persuades (see 722). Solomon Pappaiah adds that such a person is useless to the world, extending the loss from the individual to society. The sandhi text reads “நல்லவையு / ணன்கு.”

tamil:
கல்லா தவரின் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்தும்
நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்.
transliteration:
Kallaa thavarin kadaiyenba katrarindhum
Nallaa ravaiyanju vaar.
current_meaning: People who have studied and understood, yet dread an assembly of good people, are said to rank even lower than the unlearned.
elementary_explanation: If a kid knows the answer but stays quiet because they’re scared, it’s as if they never knew it. It might even be worse, because a kid who doesn’t know can at least ask a question.
university_explanation: Kaṭai means “the lowest,” so kallātavariṉ kaṭai is “lower than the unlearned.” The verb eṉpa (“they say”) presents the judgement as the verdict of the wise. Kaṟṟu aṟintum, “though they have learned and understood,” stresses both study and understanding, so the failure is purely a failure of nerve. Solomon Pappaiah reads avai añcuvār as those so afraid that they do not even go to the assembly. The ranking is harsh because the unlearned at least lack the means, while the learned coward wastes what he has. Variant: thirukkural-thamizh’s sandhi text reads “கல்லா தவரிற் கடையென்ப கற்றறிந்து / நல்லா ரவையஞ்சு வார்,” where the final -um of கற்றறிந்தும் is absorbed before ந; ytamizh prints the separated form கற்றறிந்தும்.

tamil:
உளரெனினும் இல்லாரொடு ஒப்பர் களன்அஞ்சிக்
கற்ற செலச்சொல்லா தார்.
transliteration:
Ulareninum illaarodu oppar kalananjik
Katra selachchollaa thaar.
current_meaning: People who fear the assembly and so cannot pass on what they have learned in a way that reaches the hearers are like the dead, even though they are alive.
elementary_explanation: A lamp that is never switched on might as well not be there. When fear stops you from ever sharing what you know, it is as if that part of you isn’t there at all.
university_explanation: Uḷar eṉiṉum (“though they exist, are alive”) and illārotu oppar (“they are equal to those who are not”) set being against non-being. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read illār as the dead. Kaḷaṉ (kaḷam, “arena, place of assembly”) stands in for avai for variety, and añci (“fearing”) names the cause. The closing phrase kaṟṟa cela-c-collātār repeats the formula of 722 and 724 and ties the chapter together: to learn but not to pass it on is a kind of death. The sandhi text reads “உளரெனினு மில்லாரொ டொப்பர் களனஞ்சிக்.”

tamil:
தள்ளா விளையுளும் தக்காரும் தாழ்விலாச்
செல்வரும் சேர்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Thallaa vilaiyulum thakkaarum thaazhvilaach
chelvarum servadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country is one where three things come together: harvests that never fail, people of real worth, and wealthy citizens whose riches do not decline.
elementary_explanation: Think of a good neighbourhood. The gardens always grow food, there are wise grown-ups you can ask for help, and the shopkeepers do well enough to keep their shops open. When all three are there together, it feels like a real home. Valluvar says a country is the same.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of naadu (the realm or territory), the third of the six angas (limbs) of kingship listed in kural 381, and it begins with a definition by constituents. Thallaa vilaiyul is literally ‘produce that does not fail’ (thal, to reject or fall off), thakkaar are ‘the worthy’, whom Parimelazhagar glosses as men of virtue and learning, and thaazhvilaa chelvar are ‘the wealthy without decline’, whom he identifies as merchants whose stock never runs out; Pope’s prose gloss follows him in naming merchants. Modern commentators widen the reading: Solomon Pappaiah turns the first term into the labourers who produce the harvest and the third into the unselfish rich, while Kalaignar reads the wealthy as those who do not squander riches on evil ends. The verb servadhu (that in which they gather together) makes the point that a land is defined by the coexistence of these groups, not by any one of them. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘விளையுளுந் தக்காருந்’ and ‘செல்வருஞ்’, which divide into the same words.

tamil:
பெரும்பொருளால் பெட்டக்க தாகி அருங்கேட்டால்
ஆற்ற விளைவது நாடு.
transliteration:
Perumporulaal pettakka thaaki arungettaal
aatra vilaivadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country is so rich that others desire it, is free from ruinous calamities, and yields a very large harvest.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a garden so lovely and full of fruit that everyone in town wishes it were theirs. It is not flooded or eaten by pests, and every year it gives more than enough. That is what a good country is like.
university_explanation: Perumporul is ‘great wealth’, and pettakkadhu means ‘that which is desirable’; Parimelazhagar takes the desire to be that of other kingdoms, so the kural admits that a rich land will be coveted, which prepares for the next chapter on fortification (Aran). Arungettaal is read by Parimelazhagar as arum-kedu, ‘with destructive causes being absent’ (arumai here meaning scarcity or absence), and Solomon Pappaiah lists the traditional calamities meant: excessive rain, drought, wild beasts, harmful birds and misrule. Aatra vilaivadhu means ‘yielding abundantly’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read pettakkadhu more generally as ‘praised and desired by all’. The sandhi-joined text runs the words together as ‘பெட்டக்க தாகி யருங்கேட்டா லாற்ற’, with no change in meaning.

tamil:
பொறையொருங்கு மேல்வருங்கால் தாங்கி இறைவற்கு
இறையொருங்கு நேர்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Poraiyorungu melvarungaal thaangi iraivarku
iraiyorungu nervadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country can carry a heavy load when it suddenly falls on it all at once, and still pay its ruler his full dues.
elementary_explanation: Picture a strong family. When cousins suddenly arrive because their house was flooded, the family makes room and shares its food, and it still pays its bills on time. A good country is strong in the same way.
university_explanation: Porai is ‘burden’ and orungu ‘all together’, so the first line describes a load that arrives all at once. Parimelazhagar specifies the load as people fleeing from neighbouring lands in distress, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, Pappaiah adding refugees from war and natural disaster. The second line plays on the double sense of irai: iraivan is the king and irai is the tax due to him, so a land ‘yields fully the king’s due to the king’ (iraivarku irai orungu nervadhu). The kural therefore measures a country’s strength by its surplus, since only a land with reserves can absorb strangers and still pay its revenue gladly. The sandhi text reads ‘மேல்வருங்காற் றாங்கி யிறைவற் கிறையொருங்கு’, the same words joined.

tamil:
உறுபசியும் ஓவாப் பிணியும் செறுபகையும்
சேரா தியல்வது நாடு.
transliteration:
Urupasiyum ovaap piniyum serupakaiyum
seraa thiyalvadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country runs its course untouched by crushing hunger, endless disease and destructive enemies.
elementary_explanation: A happy home is one where nobody goes to bed hungry, nobody is sick all the time, and nobody is afraid of bullies breaking in. Valluvar says a good country is a whole land like that.
university_explanation: The kural names the classic triad of public calamity: urupasi (severe hunger, famine), ovaap pini (disease that does not cease, that is, epidemic) and serupakai (enemies who destroy). Parimelazhagar notes that the third means enemies who come from outside and attack, since internal enmity is treated separately in the next kural. The verb iyalvadhu (that which goes on, continues) suggests a lasting condition rather than a single lucky year. The same trio of famine, pestilence and war recurs in Sanskrit, biblical and Greek accounts of disaster, which makes this one of the most widely shared ideas in the chapter. The sandhi text reads ‘உறுபசியு மோவாப் பிணியுஞ் செறுபகையுஞ்’.

tamil:
பல்குழுவும் பாழ்செய்யும் உட்பகையும் வேந்தலைக்கும்
கொல்குறும்பும் இல்லது நாடு.
transliteration:
Palkuzhuvum paazhseyyum utpakaiyum vendhalaikkum
kolkurumpum illadhu naadu.
current_meaning: A true country is free of rival factions, of enemies within who bring ruin, and of murderous gangs that trouble the ruler.
elementary_explanation: A sports team can have the best players, but if they split into little groups that fight each other, and some even help the other side, they will lose. A country is the same: it needs its people to pull together.
university_explanation: Where kural 734 dealt with dangers from outside, this one turns to dangers from within. Palkuzhu is ‘many groups’, which Parimelazhagar reads as factions that quarrel among themselves, paazhseyyum utpakai is ‘internal enmity that works ruin’, and vendhalaikkum kolkurumpu is ‘murderous petty chiefs (or bands) that harass the king’; kurumpu can mean a small hill-chief or a gang of marauders. Solomon Pappaiah modernises the list as caste, religious and political factions, disloyal party members, and local strongmen. The theme is developed fully in chapter 89 (Utpakai, Internal Enmity). The ytamizh text prints the last word as ‘இல்லத’, which appears to be a typographical slip for the standard ‘இல்லது’ found in the sandhi text and other editions.

tamil:
கேடறியாக் கெட்ட இடத்தும் வளங்குன்றா
நாடென்ப நாட்டின் தலை.
transliteration:
Kedariyaak ketta idaththum valangundraa
naadenpa naattin thalai.
current_meaning: The wise say the best of all countries is one that does not know ruin, and even when harm does come, does not lose its richness.
elementary_explanation: A strong tree is rarely hurt by storms, and even when a branch breaks, it keeps giving fruit. The best country is like that tree: hardly ever harmed, and quick to stay fruitful even when it is.
university_explanation: The kural has two degrees of excellence: kedariyaa (‘not knowing ruin’) and, failing that, ketta idaththum valam kundraa (‘even when ruined, its richness does not decline’). Parimelazhagar takes the ruin to be damage from enemies, and Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow him, while Kalaignar reads it as any kind of harm that the land’s resources are great enough to repair. Enpa (‘they say’) marks the judgment as the view of the learned, and naattin thalai means ‘the head, or foremost, of lands’. The idea is resilience: the best land is judged not only by its good years but by how it comes through bad ones. The ytamizh text reads ‘நாட்டின் தலை’ and the sandhi text ‘நாட்டிற் தலை’, a difference of joining only.

tamil:
இருபுனலும் வாய்ந்த மலையும் வருபுனலும்
வல்லரணும் நாட்டிற்கு உறுப்பு.
transliteration:
Irupunalum vaaindha malaiyum varupunalum
vallaranum naattirku uruppu.
current_meaning: The limbs of a country are its two kinds of water, well-placed hills, the water that flows down from them, and a strong fortress.
elementary_explanation: A castle in a story often sits by a river, with hills behind it, springs nearby and high walls around it. Water keeps people alive, and hills and walls keep them safe. Valluvar says a country needs all of these, like a body needs arms and legs.
university_explanation: Uruppu means ‘limb’ or ‘organ’, so the kural presents the natural features of a land as parts of a living body. Parimelazhagar reads irupunal (‘the two waters’) as water from below (springs, wells) and water from above (rain), and varupunal (‘the water that comes’) as rivers flowing from the hills; the hills themselves are vaaindha (well situated) because they feed the rivers and shelter the land. Kalaignar instead reads irupunal as river and sea, and varupunal as rain. Vallaran, the ‘strong fortress’, anticipates the next chapter, Aran, where hills, water and forest reappear as natural defences. The sandhi text reads ‘வல்லரணு நாட்டிற் குறுப்பு’.

tamil:
பிணியின்மை செல்வம் விளைவின்பம் ஏமம்
அணியென்ப நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து.
transliteration:
Piniyinmai selvam vilaivinpam emam
aniyenpa naattirkiv vaindhu.
current_meaning: The learned say a country has five ornaments: freedom from disease, wealth, good harvests, happiness and security.
elementary_explanation: A birthday cake looks best with candles, icing, fruit, sprinkles and a name on top. A country has its own five decorations: healthy people, enough money, good crops, happy faces and safe streets.
university_explanation: Ani means ‘ornament’ or ‘jewel’, so where kural 737 listed the land’s limbs (uruppu), this one lists its adornments. The five are piniyinmai (absence of disease), selvam (wealth), vilaivu (produce), inpam (enjoyment, happiness) and emam (safety, protection); Parimelazhagar glosses emam as the protection given to subjects. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pope follow the same five, while some modern readers join vilaivu and inpam as ‘the joy of harvest’. The verse sums up the chapter’s positive ideal in a single list. The ytamizh text prints the second line as ‘அணியென்ப நாட்டிவ் வைந்து’, but the sandhi text and the standard editions read ‘நாட்டிற்கிவ் வைந்து’ (naattirku + iv + aindhu, ‘these five for a land’), which is needed for the metre and is followed here.

tamil:
நாடென்ப நாடா வளத்தன நாடல்ல
நாட வளந்தரு நாடு.
transliteration:
Naadenpa naadaa valaththana naadalla
naada valandharu naadu.
current_meaning: The learned call those lands true countries whose wealth comes without being sought; a land that gives wealth only when laboriously sought is not a true country.
elementary_explanation: Some gardens grow fruit almost by themselves because the soil and rain are just right. Other gardens need you to dig, water and fight weeds every day for a tiny crop. Valluvar says the best country is like the first garden.
university_explanation: The kural is built on a pun between naadu (‘country’) and the verb naadu (‘to seek, to search for’): naadaa valaththana are lands ‘whose wealth is not sought’, and naada valandharu naadu is a land ‘that gives wealth only when sought’. Parimelazhagar explains that the best lands produce their riches by natural endowment, without great exertion by the inhabitants, while lands that yield only to heavy labour are not counted as countries in the full sense. The line is not a praise of idleness, since the Kural elsewhere (chapter 62, Aalvinaiyudaimai) insists on effort; it is a judgment on natural endowment. Kalaignar makes this explicit by contrasting lands naturally rich with lands that prosper only through constant struggle.

tamil:
ஆங்கமை வெய்தியக் கண்ணும் பயமின்றே
வேந்தமை வில்லாத நாடு.
transliteration:
Aangamai veydhiyak kannum payamindre
vendhamai villaadha naadu.
current_meaning: Even if a land has every good quality described above, it is of no use if it lacks a fitting ruler in harmony with it.
elementary_explanation: You can have the best football, the greenest field and the fastest players, but without a good captain who works well with the team, you will not win. A country with every treasure still needs a good leader.
university_explanation: The chapter ends by subordinating everything it has praised to kingship. Aangu amaivu eydhiya kannum means ‘even when it has attained all the excellences set out there’ (in the previous nine kurals), and payam indre means ‘it is without fruit’. The key compound vendhamaivu is read by Parimelazhagar as ‘harmony, or fitness, between king and subjects’, which Pope follows with ‘not with its king at peace’; Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read it more simply as ‘a good king or good government’, and Solomon Pappaiah as a government with love for its citizens. Either way, the verse links this chapter back to the Kural’s section on kingship (Arasiyal) and warns that natural wealth without right rule is wasted. The sandhi text agrees with ytamizh word for word.

tamil:
ஆற்று பவர்க்கும் அரண்பொருள் அஞ்சித்தற்
போற்று பவர்க்கும் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Aatru pavarkkum aranporul anjiththar
potru pavarkkum porul.
current_meaning: A fortress is a prized possession both for the king who marches out to attack and for the one who, fearing attack, shelters behind it to protect himself.
elementary_explanation: Think of a tree house with a strong ladder. When you want to go out and play a game of tag, it is your safe base to run out from. When it starts to rain or a big dog chases you, it is the place you run back into. Valluvar says a fort is useful in both ways, for going out and for staying safe.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the Kural’s treatment of aran (fortification), the last of the six angas (limbs) of the state listed in kural 381 (padai, kudi, koozh, amaichu, natpu, aran). The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: aatrupavar are ‘those who act’, which Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) take as those who go out to make war on others, while anjith than potrupavar are ‘those who, fearing, guard themselves’, the besieged who seek shelter. The word porul is used twice, first as ‘a thing of value’ (aran porul, ‘the fort is a treasure’) and then as the predicate, a deliberate play on the same word that also names the whole second book of the Kural (Porutpaal). The point is that a fortress is not merely defensive: it is a base of operations for offense and a refuge in weakness alike. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘ஆற்று பவர்க்கு மரண்பொரு ளஞ்சித்தற்’, which divides into the same words as the ytamizh.com text.

tamil:
மணிநீரும் மண்ணும் மலையும் அணிநிழற்
காடும் உடைய தரண்.
transliteration:
Maninheerum mannum malaiyum aninizhar
kaadum udaiya tharan.
current_meaning: A true fortress has water as clear as a gem, open ground, hills and a forest with thick shade.
elementary_explanation: Imagine building a pillow fort. It is best to put it behind the sofa, beside a blanket ‘river’, with a big armchair ‘mountain’ next to it and lots of cushions like a forest. Anyone sneaking up has to cross all of that first. Valluvar says the best forts use nature in the same way: water, open ground, hills and forest.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar lists the natural defenses (iyarkai aran) that should surround a fort: mani neer (water clear as a gem, i.e. a moat or lake that never dries), mann (land, glossed by Varadarasanar and Pappaiah as open ground with no cover for an attacker), malai (hill) and ani nizhal kaadu (forest of beautiful or dense shade). Parimelazhagar and the later commentators read these as four types of fort: neer aran, nila aran, malai aran and kaattu aran. Pappaiah states this directly. The list closely parallels the Sanskrit arthashastra classification into water-fort (audaka), mountain-fort (parvata), desert or open-land fort (dhanvana) and forest-fort (vanadurga), which suggests a shared South Asian military science that the next couplet calls simply ‘the treatise’ (nool). Kalaignar reads mani neer as a deep, wide moat. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘மணிநீரு மண்ணு மலையு மணிநிழற் / காடு முடைய தரண்’, which divides into the same words.

tamil:
உயர்வகலம் திண்மை அருமைஇந் நான்கின்
அமைவரண் என்றுரைக்கும் நூல்.
transliteration:
Uyarvakalam thinmai arumaiin naankin
amaivaran endruraikkum nool.
current_meaning: The treatises say that a fort is a wall that has four qualities together: height, breadth, strength and inaccessibility.
elementary_explanation: A good sandcastle wall has to be tall so the waves can’t jump over it, thick so they can’t push through, packed hard so it doesn’t crumble, and hard to reach, maybe behind a ditch. If any one of these is missing, the sea gets in. Valluvar says the old books on forts ask for the same four things.
university_explanation: After the natural defenses (742), Valluvar turns to the man-made wall (seyarkai aran, as Pappaiah calls it) and gives its four standard qualities: uyarvu (height, so that it cannot be scaled), akalam (breadth, which Pappaiah explains as room for defenders to stand and move on the rampart), thinmai (solidity, so that it cannot be battered down) and arumai (difficulty or inaccessibility). Parimelazhagar’s tradition explains arumai as the difficulty of approach created by engines and traps (pori) set on the walls, a reading that Pappaiah follows. The phrase endru uraikkum nool, ‘so says the treatise’, is one of the places where Valluvar openly cites earlier military and political science. Commentators link it to the arthashastra tradition, whose fort specifications (for example, a rampart ‘six dandas high and twice as much broad’) are very similar. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘உயர்வகலந் திண்மை யருமையிந் நான்கி / னமைவர ணென்றுரைக்கு நூல்’.

tamil:
சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி உறுபகை
ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்.
transliteration:
Sirukaappir peridaththa thaaki urupakai
ookkam azhippa tharan.
current_meaning: A fortress should have only a few points that need guarding but plenty of space inside, and it should break the spirit of any enemy that attacks it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a playground fort with just one small doorway and lots of room inside. You only need one friend at the door to keep watch, while everyone else can play inside. And anyone who tries to get in soon gives up, because the doorway is so hard to rush. That is Valluvar’s kind of fort.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two design principles against each other: siru kaappu (small guard-length, i.e. few places that need to be defended) and per idam (large interior space). The commentators all explain this as a narrow, easily held perimeter or entrance around a spacious interior; Kalaignar says that the part to be protected is small while the inside is wide. The second line gives the purpose: urupakai ookkam azhippathu, ‘that which destroys the zeal of the strong enemy who comes against it’. Pappaiah glosses this as filling the besiegers with dismay. The idea is psychological as much as structural: a well-designed fort defeats the attacker’s morale before it defeats his army. Parimelazhagar treats the chapter’s verses from 743 on as a list of the defining marks (ilakkanam) of a man-made fort. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘சிறுகாப்பிற் பேரிடத்த தாகி யுறுபகை / யூக்க மழிப்ப தரண்’.

tamil:
கொளற்கரிதாய்க் கொண்டகூழ்த் தாகி அகத்தார்
நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது அரண்.
transliteration:
Kolarkarithaaik kondakoozhth thaaki akaththaar
nilaikkelithaam neerathu aran.
current_meaning: A fortress should be hard to capture, well stocked with food, and easy for the people inside to hold and fight from.
elementary_explanation: If you are playing a long game of capture-the-flag, your base needs three things. It should be hard for the other team to get into, it should have snacks and water so you don’t have to leave, and it should be easy for your own team to move around in. Valluvar says a real fort needs the same three things.
university_explanation: The couplet names three conditions. Kolarku arithaai means ‘hard to take’; Pappaiah adds ‘even under a siege of many days’. Konda koozhthu aagi means ‘holding provisions’. Koozh (literally gruel or food) is the same word that names the Koozhiyal (the section on wealth and resources) in some divisions of the Porutpaal, and here it means stored food. Akaththaar nilaikku elithaam means ‘easy for those within to hold their position’. Varadarasanar reads this as easy for the defenders to stay in, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as convenient for the defenders to fight from. The final neerathu (‘of such a nature’) marks the three conditions as the fort’s defining nature. The ytamizh text reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதாம் நீரது’, and the sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org reads ‘நிலைக்கெளிதா நீர தரண்’. These are orthographic variants of the same words.

tamil:
எல்லாப் பொருளும் உடைத்தாய் இடத்துதவும்
நல்லாள் உடையது அரண்.
transliteration:
Ellaap porulum udaiththaai idaththuthavum
nallaal udaiyathu aran.
current_meaning: A true fortress holds everything that might be needed and has brave, good men who will help when danger comes.
elementary_explanation: A good school on a stormy day has torches, blankets and food in the cupboard. But it also needs calm grown-ups who know what to do when the lights go out. Supplies alone are not enough; you need good people too. Valluvar says the same about a fort.
university_explanation: The first line (ellaap porulum udaiththaai, ‘having all things’) sums up the material requirements of 745, and the second line brings in the human element that the chapter’s last couplet will make decisive: idaththu uthavum nallaal, ‘good men who help at the (critical) place or time’. Idam can mean both the spot where danger arises and the moment of need, and Varadarasanar reads it as the moment of crisis in battle. Nallaal (nal + aal, ‘good person’) is read by all the commentators as brave warriors: Pappaiah speaks of heroes who can defeat enemies trying to destroy the fort from outside, and Kalaignar of strong fighters who leap into battle. The pairing of stores and soldiers reflects the arthashastra and Dharmashastra habit of listing a fort’s supplies and its garrison together. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எல்லாப் பொருளு முடைத்தா யிடத்துதவு / நல்லா ளுடைய தரண்’.

tamil:
முற்றியும் முற்றா தெறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்
பற்றற் கரியது அரண்.
transliteration:
Mutriyum mutraa therindhum araippaduththum
patrar kariyathu aran.
current_meaning: A true fortress cannot be taken by blockade, by direct assault without a blockade, or by treachery from within.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your best toy locked in a treasure box. Someone might wait outside your room for hours, or try to grab it quickly, or even trick your little brother into opening the box. A really safe box beats all three tricks. Valluvar says a real fort must be safe from waiting, grabbing and tricking.
university_explanation: The couplet lists the three ways a fort can be taken and says a true aran resists all of them: mutriyum (by besieging it all round), mutraathu erindhum (by attacking without a full siege, i.e. storming a weak point), and araippaduththum (by araippadal, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read as vanjanai, deceit or treachery, and Pappaiah as turning some of those inside into a fifth column). Pope’s English (‘mine beneath the ground’) follows the other old sense of arai as a hollow or underground passage, so there is a real divergence between treachery and undermining; the Tamil commentarial tradition generally prefers treachery. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘முற்றியு முற்றா தெறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’, where ‘எறிந்து மறைப்படுத்தும்’ is the sandhi form of ‘எறிந்தும் அறைப்படுத்தும்’, which confirms the reading araippaduththum. The inclusion of treachery points ahead to 750: the human element can undo even a physically perfect fort.

tamil:
முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப்
பற்றியார் வெல்வது அரண்.
transliteration:
Mutraatri mutri yavaraiyum patraatrip
patriyaar velvathu aran.
current_meaning: A true fortress lets those inside, holding firm to their positions, defeat even a strong army skilled at siegecraft that surrounds them.
elementary_explanation: In a game of king-of-the-hill, the one on top can hold off a crowd of climbers as long as he keeps his footing. Valluvar says a good fort works like that hill. Even when many skilled attackers surround it, the defenders who hold their ground can win.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats two roots in a tight pattern. Mutraatri mutriyavar means ‘those who besiege, being skilled (aatri) in besieging’, i.e. an expert siege force, and patraatrip patriyaar means ‘those who hold on, being able to hold (their ground)’, i.e. the defenders who do not let go of the place they occupy. Varadarasanar reads patru as the defenders’ attachment to their position, and Pappaiah as not abandoning their post. The fort is defined by its result: it is that in which the holders defeat (velvathu) even a skilled besieger. The repeated sounds (mutru, patru) make the couplet memorable. It shifts the chapter from the fort’s structure to the fort in action, preparing for 749-750. The sandhi-joined text on thirukkural-thamizh.org is ‘முற்றாற்றி முற்றி யவரையும் பற்றாற்றிப் / பற்றியார் வெல்வ தரண்’, which matches ytamizh.com.

tamil:
முனைமுகத்து மாற்றலர் சாய வினைமுகத்து
வீறெய்தி மாண்ட தரண்.
transliteration:
Munaimukaththu maatralar saaya vinaimukaththu
veereythi maanda tharan.
current_meaning: A true fortress wins fame through the fighting skill of its defenders, which brings the enemy down at the very front line of battle.
elementary_explanation: A castle becomes famous not just because its walls are pretty but because of the brave defenders who stopped every attack at the gate. People tell stories about what they did there. Valluvar says a fort gets its greatness from the deeds done in its defense.
university_explanation: The couplet sets munaimukam (the battle-front) against vinaimukam (the field of action or operations): the enemy (maatralar) falls (saaya) at the front because of what the defenders do, and through those deeds the fort attains distinction (veeru eythi) and excellence (maanda). Pappaiah notes that the enemy is destroyed ‘as soon as battle begins’, and Kalaignar stresses attacks launched from within. Veeru, ‘pride, distinction, uniqueness’, suggests that a fort’s fame comes from the deeds done in its defense rather than from its stones. The couplet is thus the bridge between the structural couplets (742-747) and the conclusion in 750 that without vinai maatchi (excellence in action) no fort exists at all. The repetition of mukaththu (‘at the face of’) in both halves is a characteristic Kural device. The sandhi-joined text is identical in wording to the ytamizh.com reading.

tamil:
எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி
இல்லார்கண் இல்லது அரண்.
transliteration:
Enaimaatchith thaakiyak kannum vinaimaatchi
illaarkan illathu aran.
current_meaning: However excellent a fortress may be, it is no fortress at all in the hands of people who lack skill and vigor in action.
elementary_explanation: You could have the best football in the world, but if nobody on your team can kick, you will still lose. A fort is the same. The tallest walls are useless if the people inside don’t know how to defend them. Valluvar ends the chapter by saying that people matter more than walls.
university_explanation: The closing couplet undercuts everything before it. Enai maatchiththu aakiya kannum means ‘even when it has every kind of excellence’, summing up the natural defenses, walls, provisions and garrison of 742-749. Yet it is illathu, ‘non-existent’, among those who lack vinai maatchi, excellence in action. Varadarasanar glosses vinai maatchi as skill in the ways of action, Pappaiah as the ability to understand and act against the enemy, and Kalaignar simply says that if those inside are incompetent there is no use at all. The play on maatchi (‘excellence’) in both lines sets the fort’s excellence against its holders’ excellence, and the holders win. Pope’s verse rendering (‘To craven souls no fortress strength supplies’) makes the lack a matter of courage, while the Tamil commentators stress practical competence more broadly. The ytamizh.com Varadarasanar gloss ends with the words ‘பொருள் செயல்வகை’, the title of the next chapter, which appears to be a page artifact rather than part of the commentary. The sandhi-joined text reads ‘எனைமாட்சித் தாகியக் கண்ணும் வினைமாட்சி / யில்லார்க ணில்ல தரண்’.
